title: NVIDIA Cosmos3-H-Dreams: Bringing Clinical Surgery to Life Through Generative Simulation
abstract: Back to Articles NVIDIA Cosmos3-H-Dreams: Bringing Clinical Surgery to Life Through Generative Simulation Enterprise + Article Published October 20, 2026 Upvote - Lukas Zbinden lzbinden Follow nvidia Javier Gamazo javirk1 Follow nvidia Nigel Nelson nigeln Follow nvidia Mostafa Toloui mtoloui Follow nvidia Sean Huver shuver Follow nvidia Picture moving the Cadiere grasper, grasping the gallbladder, and lifting it, all within a generated surgical scene that responds in real time. Today, we take the next step and introduce Cosmos3-H-Dreams, bringing interactive generative simulation to the visual and procedural complexity of clinical surgery with our most convincing in-body imagery to date. Our first Cosmos-H-Dreams release, built on Cosmos-Predict2.5, brought interactive generative simulation to dVRK tabletop suturing, a foundational proving ground for surgical robotics. As world foundation model (WFM), Cosmos-H-Dreams demonstrated an alternative to numerical simulation: rather than explicitly modeling scene geometry, tissue deformation, and physical interactions, it learned visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics, yielding interactive tabletop task simulation with high realism. Today, Cosmos3-H-Dreams advances this capability by learning from video and robot kinematics recording during clinical procedures on the CMR Surgical Versius platform. To our knowledge, this is the first real-time generative surgical simulator trained on clinical cholecystectomy recordings to support live kinematic control. Powered by Cosmos 3 and accelerated with FlashDreams, NVIDIA’s accelerated streaming-inference library, Cosmos3-H-Dreams runs interactively on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. 1. From Tabletop Tasks to Clinical Scenes In a controlled tabletop environment like that of Cosmos-H-Dreams, instruments operate against a relatively simple background. Inside the human body, however, small instrument movements can affect an entire scene: tissue stretches under traction, reflections shift, structures become occluded, and smoke changes visibility. Given an initial image and supplied tool actions, a generative simulator must capture these responses while preserving the anatomy and instruments as it generates each new block of video. Small errors can accumulate over time, gradually changing instrument geometry or anatomical structure, making temporal consistency essential. Visual realism is therefore a starting point for validation, not proof of biomechanical accuracy. The generated scene must also follow the controls: translation, rotation, and gripper commands should produce coherent anatomical consequences. A plausible-looking rollout that ignores those commands cannot serve as an interactive environment. Maintaining this fidelity and responsiveness in a live control loop requires low latency generation. Cosmos3-H-Dreams addresses this setting through a model specialized for clinical cholecystectomy and distilled for real-time generation, bringing action-conditioned interaction into scenes with complex anatomy, tissue motion, and occlusion. 2. What is New in Cosmos3-H-Dreams? 2.1 A Cosmos 3 Foundation and Richer Surgical Controls Cosmos3-H-Dreams builds on Cosmos3-H-Embodied-Nano , a 16-billion-parameter model pretrained on Open-H-Embodiment , and specializes a bidirectional teacher on curated cholecystectomy video and kinematics. Sample selection targets two visible, engaged instruments, a left Cadiere grasper and a right monopolar hook, and limits camera commands to emphasize instrument-driven interaction. The model uses 28 action dimensions: pose and gripper information for both arms, plus energy controls, thumbstick axes and thumbstick buttons. Training uses 832 x 480 video with actions aligned at 10 Hz; that sampling rate is distinct from runtime generation throughput. 2.2 From Teacher to Four-Step and Two-Step Students Cosmos3-H-Dreams combines a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long autoregressive rollouts with accelerated streaming inference through FlashDreams. We first adapt the bidirectional teacher on 24 future frames, then extend the horizon to 72 frames, 2.4 and 7.2 seconds at 10 Hz. This gives the teacher longer sequences over which to learn surgical dynamics. Next, distillation turns the bidirectional teacher into a causal student that can generate video in short blocks as new actions arrive. Causal teacher forcing prepares the student for sequential generation using recorded context. Self-Forcing then trains it on its own generated context, guided by the teacher and a learned critic. This helps address the accumulation of errors during interactive rollouts. The first released student uses four denoising steps per generated block. We then train that student further with a two-step schedule to produce the second release checkpoint. The two-step model is separately trained, not simply the four-step model run with fewer sampling steps. Fewer denoising steps results in faster inference time at the expense of lower visual quality. Both checkpoints let developers explore the balance between visual quality and inference cost. 2.3 Streaming through FlashDreams FlashDreams supplies the accelerated streaming runtime. Long rollouts also require managing the model’s attention history. The Cosmos3-H-Dreams integration uses an adapted FadeMem module that consolidates the growing key/value cache during long rollouts. This complements Self-Forcing: distillation addresses how the model learns from its generated history, while cache consolidation addresses how that history is stored during streaming generation. 3. Exploring Unseen Trajectories During a clinical procedure there may be complications or some room for the surgeon to perform “novel” movements. Therefore, a simulator must be able to generalize beyond the training data, and produce coherent frames with unseen movements. The demonstrations below show Cosmos3-H-Dreams generating different cholecystectomy scenes conditioned on instrument actions recorded with a VR headset. The two videos begin with the same initial frame but follow different action sequences illustrating how instrument control leads to distinct continuations of the same scene with physically accurate tissue deformations. Furthermore, these rollouts allow us to inspect whether instruments follow the controls, whether tissue responds coherently to interaction, and whether anatomical and instrument appearance remain consistent over time. 4. Adapting to Your Own Data and Controller Cosmos3-H-Dreams includes four-step and two-step checkpoints for cholecystectomy. The system can be adapted to other datasets and embodiments with synchronized video and compatible action representations. To train a real-time student model on your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and Self-Forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide . It describes data preparation, public teacher-training tools, and the distillation stages. Controller integrations must use the same action conventions and normalization as training. 5. What is Next The advance in visual realism opens several research directions: Model the full procedure. Expand coverage and temporal consistency so all phases of cholecystectomy can be explored systematically, with clear task boundaries and success criteria. Connect generative and numerical simulation. Combine learned visual realism with explicit geometry, contact and tissue mechanics. Numerical models and measured data could help constrain and validate deformation, making simulation behavior inspectable as well as convincing. Evaluate with surgeons. Assess anatomical accuracy, instrument behavior and tissue response, turning expert feedback into reproducible benchmarks. Support more instruments. Move beyond two controlled tools to richer coordination, occlusion and interaction. Develop autonomous surgical policies.

title: FairStress: A deeper evaluation of fairness in LLM decision-making
abstract: Back to Articles FairStress: A deeper evaluation of fairness in LLM decision-making Enterprise Article Published October 20, 2026 Upvote 2 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Tech Report | 🤗 Data | 💻 Code Today we’re introducing FairStress , a benchmark for measuring demographic fairness in LLMs beyond the choice a model ultimately makes in decisions impacting people. FairStress is available for download, and we’re also building it into Olmo-eval , our open workbench for running and comparing model evaluations. Models are increasingly being used in high-stakes settings where their outputs can affect people’s opportunities, resources, and care, from screening job applicants and approving loans to prioritizing patients for treatment and evaluating students for admissions. Standard demographic fairness benchmarks often test whether a model selects the same candidate in otherwise identical scenarios after the candidates’ demographic identities are swapped. For example, if one job candidate has clearly stronger experience and qualifications, does the model still choose that candidate when the stronger candidate is Black in one version of the scenario and white in the other, with the qualifications held constant? Arriving at the same answer in two versions of a scenario can hide meaningful differences in how readily a model changes that decision when challenged, however. Suppose Candidate A is clearly stronger and the model selects A whether A is Black or white. That looks fair at the output level, but if the model is then presented with a persuasive argument – for example, that Candidate B is preferred by senior leadership, or that people from B’s demographic group have historically been overlooked – it may switch away from the stronger candidate much more readily in one version of the scenario than the other. FairStress is designed to measure these hidden asymmetries. Across open-weight and frontier models including Olmo, Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Claude, and the GPT family, and across multiple stages of training, we find that the same persuasive arguments – which we call adversarial prefixes – can make models more or less likely to change their decisions depending on which demographic group the argument favors. We also find differences in how models explain decisions involving demographic information – and in their internal activation patterns – across domains including hiring, lending, healthcare, education, and housing. With FairStress, our target is symmetric fairness —when the evidence supports a decision, a model should apply the same criteria and be equally resistant to changing that decision regardless of which demographic group benefits. This reflects a particular definition of fairness centered on equality. All else equal, people of different identities should be equally likely to be selected; when one candidate is clearly the strongest choice, identity should not change that likelihood; and well-supported decisions should be equally robust to adversarial prefixes regardless of which group benefits. FairStress does not attempt to capture every conception of fairness. An equity-based approach, for example, might treat historical discrimination or underrepresentation as relevant to a decision and therefore favor a minority candidate even when other factors are held constant. Measuring fairness beyond the final answer FairStress contains 300 realistic two-candidate decision scenarios across 29 domains including hiring, healthcare, lending, education, housing, and criminal justice. For example, one scenario asks a model to choose between two candidates for a mechanical engineering job, while another asks which of two patients should receive the last unit of a scarce medication. Some FairStress scenarios have a clearly stronger candidate whose profile better satisfies the stated criteria. That lets us test whether demographic information changes how often a model selects the candidate best supported by the evidence. Other scenarios are deliberately ambiguous—both candidates are strong in different, hard-to-compare ways so there’s no objectively better choice. These cases let us examine which candidate a model favors when the evidence does not clearly point to one over the other. FairStress also varies how explicitly demographic identity is presented, from no identity information to a demographically coded name, an indirectly implied identity, or an explicit demographic label. This allows us to test whether demographic differences in model behavior emerge only when identity is stated outright or also when it’s conveyed subtly. Our benchmark goes further by testing how stable models’ decisions are when challenged by adversarial prefixes. These statements draw on authority, social consensus, purported evidence, legal concerns, historical disadvantage, and other forms of persuasion—for example, “A senior leader has privately reviewed the files and recommended Candidate B for this role.” We then measure whether a model changes its choice in response. Each prefix has a matched version that makes the same kind of case for the other candidate, allowing us to robustly test whether the same argument has different effects depending on which candidate it supports. Combining these variations in demographic identity and prefix expands FairStress’ 300 scenarios into more than 13 million test cases. Alongside the full benchmark, we’ve developed FairStress-Core, a 50K-item subset selected using item response theory, following our Fluid Benchmarking approach. It’s designed to make evaluation faster and less computationally expensive while retaining much of the full benchmark’s ability to reveal differences in model behavior. Models do not always hold correct answers equally In our experiments with FairStress, we found little difference in model behavior when prompts contained no demographic information. When one candidate was clearly stronger, models selected that candidate at nearly the same rate across otherwise equivalent versions of the scenario. On ambiguous cases, where neither candidate was objectively stronger, the models’ choices were also close to evenly split. As demographic identity became more explicit in the prompt, however, model behavior became less symmetric. For example, suppose Candidate A is clearly better qualified than Candidate B. When A was majority-coded – carrying the conventionally advantaged identity in that comparison, such as white, male, or heterosexual – and B was minority-coded, a prefix favoring B was more likely to make the model switch from the stronger candidate to the weaker one. When A was minority-coded and B was majority-coded, with their qualifications held fixed, the same kind of prefix favoring B was less likely to make the model abandon its correct choice of A. We describe this pattern as anti-stereotypical over-correction : in these comparisons, models were more willing to abandon a correct decision when doing so favored a minority-coded candidate. The concern is that demographic identity changes how consistently a model follows the evidence, even when one candidate is clearly better qualified. In this hiring example, Tülu 3.1 8B selected the Black transgender woman in both versions of the scenario. When her résumé was weaker, its explanation emphasized growth potential and a diverse background despite missing certifications. When her résumé was stronger, it emphasized experience and certification. Mean gaps between minority-coded and majority-coded candidates across 15 models, evaluated in the 19 domains shared by all four identity conditions. Values are in percentage points. Positive values indicate differences favoring minority-coded candidates; zero indicates equal rates across groups. These differences also appeared when demographic identity was implied rather than stated outright. Across the 15 models evaluated on the full benchmark, the average gap in abandoning correct answers was 6.

title: ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model
abstract:
Back to Articles ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model Enterprise Article Published October 20, 2026 Upvote 18 +12 Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan ashwath-vaithina Follow ibm-research Vatche Isahagian Vatche Follow ibm-research Vinod Muthusamy vinodmut Follow ibm-research Jayaram Radhakrishnan jayaramkr Follow ibm-research Evelyn Duesterwald evduester Follow ibm-research Gaodan Fang gaodan-fang Follow ibm-research Punleuk Oum illeatmyhat Follow ibm-research G Thomas gsthomasx Follow ibm-research Michał Ulewicz Michal Follow ibm-research Merve Unuvar mrvnvr Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research ALTK-Evolve learns and applies a playbook using GPT-4.1, outperforming the retail entries on τ²-bench, a customer service agent benchmark—without updating model weights. Learned memory takes a basic ReAct agent with GPT-4.1 to the top Using GPT-4.1, an older, non-reasoning model, a basic customer-service agent reaches 67.5% Pass^4 on τ²-bench retail — meaning it solves the task on all four independent attempts for 67.5% of tasks. It scores above every retail entry in our October 12, 2026 leaderboard snapshot. It runs on the benchmark's stock ReAct scaffold, with learned guidelines appended to its system prompt. ALTK-Evolve builds that playbook using GPT-4.1. It analyzes the agent's training-task attempts and uses the model to distill successes and failures into short behavioral rules: how to authenticate a customer, confirm a transaction, or handle a return. Those guidelines are then added to the agent's prompt for subsequent conversations. The same model powers both guideline extraction and the agent; no weight updates or human annotation are needed. Our previous work demonstrated this approach on coding agents. Here, we test it on customer service, where success requires following domain policies, understanding a customer's request, and executing the right tool actions. τ²-bench tests policy-bound customer service τ²-bench (from Sierra) measures how well an agent handles customer-service conversations under real constraints. Each task pairs the agent with an LLM-simulated customer who has a goal in mind, a set of domain tools (look up an order, issue a refund, rebook a flight), and a written policy document the agent must follow. The agent has to draw out the right details, stay within policy, and take the correct — often irreversible — actions; a task counts as solved only when the final database state matches the expected outcome, a strict binary reward. We use its two customer-service domains, retail and airline . We run τ²-bench's own implementation of a basic ReAct agent with a two-phase THINK → ACT loop, using gpt-4.1 as the agent model and gpt-5.5 as the customer-simulator model; 4 trials per task. The only change we make is a block of learned guidelines appended to the system prompt — everything else (policy, tools, scaffold) is stock τ²-bench. Concretely, the learned guidelines are tacked on after the domain policy as a plain markdown list: You are a customer service agent that helps users according to the policy below.
Always follow the policy strictly. Use the provided tools when needed. <policy>
# Retail agent policy As a retail agent, you can help users:
- cancel or modify pending orders
- return or exchange delivered orders
- modify their default user address
…
</policy> ## Guidelines learned from past task attempts (follow these carefully):
- Authenticate the user before taking any order-related action. If email is unavailable, verify identity via full name and zip code using the find_user_id_by_name_zip API.
- Always confirm all intended changes (modify, cancel, return, exchange) with a clear, structured summary, and require explicit user approval before executing any database-updating action.
- When processing a return or exchange, communicate the refund with an itemized breakdown and clarify refund timing — don't wait for the user to ask.
- Take one action per step: never combine a tool call with a user-facing message in the same turn, and wait for the tool's result before replying.
- Before looking a user up, parse and clean their name — e.g. split a combined handle like `daiki_johnson_9523` into first/last name — and after a couple of failed lookups, state the exact format you need.
… We extract guidelines from the agent's trajectories on τ²-bench train tasks using gpt-4.1 , the same model that powers the agent, then apply them unchanged on the held-out test set. Guidelines improve capability and reliability In a prior post , we talked about how different models / tasks require different dosage of guidance. Inline with the idea, we also evaluate different amounts of guidelines provided to the model. Each guideline carries a support count — the number of distinct training tasks it was extracted from, so higher support means a rule that generalized across more tasks rather than a one-off. We compare three configurations: baseline (no guidelines), sup3 (keep only guidelines with support ≥ 3 — a small, high-confidence core), and lossless (keep every guideline retained after consolidation, i.e. support ≥ 1). Table 1. Guideline configurations and retained guideline counts by domain. Variant Guidelines included in context Retail Airline baseline no guidelines 0 0 sup3 support n ≥ 3 (high-support core) 31 14 lossless all guidelines 292 101 The metrics we track. Every task is attempted 4 times , and we read those trials two ways: Mean Accuracy — the average success rate across the 4 trials. This is the capability axis: how often does the agent get this right? Pass^4 — the percentage of tasks that passed across all 4 trials. This measures along the reliability axis and the metric the τ²-bench leaderboard reports. It matters here because a support agent that resolves a refund 3 times out of 4 still fails a quarter of real customers — Pass^4 asks whether you can trust the agent every time, not just on average. Figure 1. Mean Accuracy and Pass^4 on held-out retail and airline tasks for agents using gpt-4.1 across four trials per task. Agent model: gpt-4.1 (user simulator: gpt-5.5 ). Table 2. Held-out agent performance using gpt-4.1 across four trials per task. Parentheses show percentage-point changes from baseline. Domain (test tasks) Config Mean Accuracy Pass^4 Retail (40) baseline 78.1% 57.5% sup3 78.8% (+0.7) 60.0% (+2.5) lossless 82.5% (+4.4) 67.5% (+10.0) Airline (20) baseline 57.5% 35.0% sup3 60.0% (+2.5) 45.0% (+10.0) lossless 65.0% (+7.5) 40.0% (+5.0) Mean Accuracy climbs in both domains — retail +4.4 pts (78.1 → 82.5) and airline +7.5 pts (57.5 → 65.0). Reliability moves further: the strict Pass^4 rises +10 pts in retail (57.5 → 67.5) and +10 pts in airline (35.0 → 45.0). And the gains come from better-informed calls, not longer conversations — we look at conversation length directly in Better performance costs more tokens, not more turns below. The best amount of guidance depends on the domain The two domains disagree about how much guidance pays off. In retail , more is better on every metric — the small sup3 core barely beats baseline on accuracy, and you need the full lossless set for the real jump. In airline the picture flips at the reliability end: lossless leads on accuracy (65% vs 60%), but the compact sup3 core (14 guidelines) is the more reliable one, taking Pass^4 to 45% against lossless's 40%. Echoing the earlier finding that delivery is a dial, not a constant , support count is a knob worth tuning per domain , not a value to hard-code. Better performance costs more tokens, not more turns Guidelines aren't free, but the cost lands where you'd expect — in prompt input tokens , not in a longer, more meandering conversation: Figure 2. Total LLM cost per conversation by domain and guideline configuration on the full base split. Table 3.

title: Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively
abstract:
Back to Articles Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 8 +2 Alvaro Moran tengomucho Follow Jingya Huang Jingya Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow Régis Pierrard regisss Follow If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla , or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU , a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu" , and you're done. Wait, what's a TPU? 🤔 TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit . TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini. TPUs are available on Google Cloud , from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale. The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in. The old way Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA ( torch_xla ). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about. To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers. Enter TorchTPU 🚀 TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command: pip install torch-tpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch . Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU. Your favourite libraries, now on TPU Transformers Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu" . That's it. from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, device_map= "tpu" , # will load model directly on the TPU )
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
inputs = tokenizer( "The future of AI is" , return_tensors= "pt" ).to( "tpu" )
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 64 ) print (tokenizer.decode(out[ 0 ], skip_special_tokens= True )) The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup. Images? Videos? Diffusers paints them on TPUs 🎨 TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu") . For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain. import torch from diffusers import StableDiffusion3Pipeline pipe = StableDiffusion3Pipeline.from_pretrained( "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-medium" , dtype=torch.bfloat16
)
pipe.to( "tpu" ) # eager mode: that's the whole change # optional: compiled mode pipe.transformer. compile (backend= "tpu" , fullgraph= True , dynamic= False ) image = pipe( "a corgi astronaut planting a flag on a pizza moon" ).images[ 0 ] The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph. Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe. Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4: TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1 MiniMax-H3 (video + audio) Qwen-Image-2.1 "The fluffy plush Hugging Face mascot from the picture, a round yellow smiling face with rosy cheeks and two little open hands, stands at the prow of an ancient Greek trireme […] Sound of crashing waves, creaking timber, wind in the rigging, distant seagulls, and a low epic orchestral swell." · 1344×768, 5.2 s, 49 steps · 188 s compiled, 262 s eager "A capybara wearing a wizard hat, reading a book by candlelight, oil painting" · 1024×1024, 40 steps · 3.5 s compiled, 8.0 s eager "A neon shop sign that reads 'QWEN IMAGE 2.1', rainy night, reflections on wet pavement" · 2048×2048, 40 steps Kernels The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost. TPU kernels are written in Pallas , which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model: from kernels import get_kernel from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM from transformers.integrations.moe import ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS repo_id = "tengomucho/ragged-dot-tpu" kernel = get_kernel(repo_id, version= 1 , trust_remote_code=[repo_id])
ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS.register( "tokamax_ragged_dot" , kernel.experts_forward)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507" , experts_implementation= "tokamax_ragged_dot" ,
) The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B. Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation. We test it so you don't have to 🧪 We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[ https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard] . The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress! It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream. If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do. Get started TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu" . TorchTPU on GitHub TPU kernels on the Hub Cloud TPU documentation We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

title: AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms
abstract:
Back to Articles AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 3 Mattt mattt Follow Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog:
a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework
that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses.
We heard from app developers who were curious about local models
but weren't always sure how to get started.
They also wanted to avoid the added complexity
of supporting multiple inference providers.
AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback. Local and hosted inference each have their strengths,
and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps.
A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task. A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out,
along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0 . Here's what changed, and what's next: A drop-in compatible API The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same:
use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app.
To get started, change your import statement: - import FoundationModels + import AnyLanguageModel The same session code then works with the system model,
with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML,
and with the hosted providers below. Over the past year, we've added several major features: Tool calling works with every provider. Guided generation works with every provider, too,
including nested @Generable types and arrays of them. Image support lets you attach images to prompts
using Foundation Models 27's syntax,
including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27. On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with
any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol,
including Core AI models. Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps. Hosted models, too Support for hosted models expanded this year, too.
AnyLanguageModel now supports: OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs Open Responses ,
for any provider with a compatible endpoint Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options Google's Gemini API Ollama Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27 Hugging Face Inference Providers ,
and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter,
through a custom base URL With Inference Providers,
you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device
with the same session code: let model = OpenAILanguageModel ( baseURL: URL (string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/" ) ! , apiKey: ProcessInfo .processInfo.environment[ "HF_TOKEN" ] ! , model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b" , apiVariant: .chatCompletions
) Hosted providers get the same features as local models:
guided generation, tool calling with streaming,
and token usage on responses. Reasoning is now part of the transcript too.
When you switch providers,
reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them. API keys come from a closure instead of a string,
so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server.
The README explains when to let people bring their own keys
and when to route requests through a proxy. AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux,
so the same code can work on a server. Open-weight models got better While we've made local models easier to use,
the models themselves have become more capable,
making the small ones a good place to start.
Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now: Gemma 4 E2B from Google,
in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at Q4_0 with quantization-aware training. LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI,
in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at Q4_K_M . Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba,
about 16 GB at 4 bits. The first two fit on an iPhone,
and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more.
Selecting the MLX model takes one line: let model = MLXLanguageModel (modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit" ) And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16.
For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers. Upgrading to 1.0 dependencies: [ .package( url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel" , from: "1.0.0" , traits: [ "MLX" ] )
] If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel , swift-huggingface ,
and swift-xet release notes
for help updating your code. Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features.
Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers. What's next Language models have proven to be a powerful tool
for building intelligence into products.
They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work.
We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities:
familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device.
Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen. Links AnyLanguageModel on GitHub swift-huggingface on GitHub swift-xet on GitHub Introducing AnyLanguageModel Introducing swift-huggingface

title: MPS in PyTorch 2.15
abstract:
Back to Articles MPS in PyTorch 2.15 Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 8 +2 Irakli Salia Isalia20 Follow Khushi Agrawal khushi-411 Follow If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads. A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors. TL;DR FP8 comes to the Mac: store float8_e4m3fn values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU! MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing. Less time per token for every LLM: single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster. More linear algebra on the GPU: complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition. Audio, video, and training get attention too: faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB. More control from Python: public MPS streams and more reliable event timing. Updated requirements: MPS now requires macOS 15 or later ; PyTorch 2.15 requires Python 3.11 or later . A peek at 2.16: attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding. What this means for you If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice: Much faster local LLMs. Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with torch.compile , Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. ( More ) Video generation that fits in memory. Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. ( More ) Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1. On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows ( reported in ComfyUI ). The same padding change fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB. FP8 weights on your Mac. FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and F.scaled_mm multiplies them directly on the GPU. ( More ) Contents Getting started FP8 comes to MPS Faster language-model decoding Linear algebra gets a boost Convolutions, padding, and training Softmax and reductions A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding More control with MPS streams More operations work on MPS A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16 Wrapping up Getting started You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix ). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why. To try the release candidate in a separate environment: uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu FP8 comes to MPS FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16. You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm , which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor: import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def quantize_fp8 ( x ): limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn). max scale = x. abs ().amax().clamp_min( 1e-12 ) / limit return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale x = torch.randn( 1 , 1024 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.randn( 1024 , 1024 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.float32)
x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x)
w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight) y = F.scaled_mm( x_fp8, w_fp8.t(), scale_a=x_scale, scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise, scale_b=w_scale, scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise, output_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
) print (y.shape, y.dtype) Faster language-model decoding Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers. Linear layers MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear , so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup . The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×. Mixture-of-experts layers A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation . In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well. For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16: import torch import torch.nn.functional as F tokens = torch.randn( 64 , 64 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.bfloat16)
weights = torch.randn( 3 , 128 , 64 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ends = torch.tensor([ 16 , 48 , 64 ], device= "mps" , dtype=torch.int32) out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(- 2 , - 1 ), offs=ends) print (out.shape) # torch.Size([64, 128]) The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile , MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second : Linear algebra gets a boost Complex-valued computations Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization , LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU: import torch a = torch.randn( 8 , 8 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.complex64)
a = a + 8 * torch.eye( 8 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.complex64)
b = torch.randn( 8 , 2 , device= "mps" , dtype=torch.complex64) lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a)
x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b) print ((a @ x - b). abs (). max ().item()) Small matrices and larger solves Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving.

title: Google Open-Sources TorchTPU, a Native PyTorch Backend for Cloud TPUs
abstract: Google has open-sourced TorchTPU , a native PyTorch backend for Cloud TPUs. It was co-developed with the PyTorch team at Meta and announced at PyTorch Conference 2026 on October 20, 2026. Existing PyTorch code targets a TPU through a standard torch.device("tpu") . TPUs now sit beside GPUs and CPUs as a native PyTorch device. Google team states that TorchTPU replaces PyTorch/XLA and recommends it for all new workloads. TorchTPU is an open-source PyTorch backend from Google and Meta that runs PyTorch models natively on TPUs. It plugs in through PyTorch’s PrivateUse1 interface . Tensors are ordinary PyTorch tensors, with no subclasses or wrappers. It runs one process per device and preserves tensor views and in-place mutations. The predecessor, PyTorch/XLA, recorded lazy-tensor graphs. Developers often added code to mark compilable regions. PyTorch/XLA also only supported pure SPMD code . TorchTPU also handles divergent MPMD execution. TorchTPU ships 3 eager modes : For peak speed, torch.compile(backend="tpu") captures the graph with TorchDynamo. It lowers through StableHLO to OpenXLA, which emits TPU machine code. Compiled executables are cached across processes, hosts and job restarts. Custom Pallas kernels are callable as standard PyTorch functions. Prebuilt Tokamax kernels and Helion tile kernels also work. Distribution uses the tpu_dist process group. It supports DDP, FSDP2 and DTensor, along with a topology-aware mesh for TPU interconnects. All figures below are self-reported by Google and partners. Install the package on a TPU VM, then pick the tpu device: The repo’s README pins torch_tpu==0.2.0 with the CPU PyTorch wheel index. Without it, pip pulls the CUDA build of torch . Full guides live at torchtpu.readthedocs.io . Check out the GitHub repo , paper , docs and Google Cloud announcement . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. title: DeepSeek Open-Sources DeepInfer, the Inference Framework Behind DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
abstract: DeepSeek has open-sourced DeepInfer , the inference framework that runs its production services. The DeepSeek DeepInfer inference framework is the engine behind DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash . It ships under the Apache 2.0 license . DeepSeek also released deepseek-recipe , its MIT-licensed token encoding and decoding layer. For developers, this is a rare look at a frontier lab’s real serving stack. DeepInfer is a high-performance inference engine from DeepSeek for its own models. According to it’s GitHub README , it powers DeepSeek’s large-scale production services. This release covers offline inference with the core features needed at scale. It was originally built primarily on vLLM , with ideas from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM. The deployment Q&A gives production context. A single cluster serves 155 trillion tokens per day. DeepSeek reports overall revenue of US$38 per GPU-hour at valley pricing. The engine stacks DeepSeek’s kernels: FlashMLA , DeepGEMM , DeepEP , TileKernels, DeepSelect and custom TileLang kernels. On top sit 5 system-level ideas. Attention uses data parallelism. The MoE layers use expert parallelism with an expert-parallel load balancer (EPLB). Decode runs EP64 to EP128 inside a supernode. Prefill uses the smallest EP that memory allows, typically EP2 to EP8. A draft model proposes 5 tokens per step. A Confidence Head predicts each draft token’s acceptance rate. The scheduler then verifies only the most valuable prefix. Per the Q&A, this cuts verified draft tokens by about 30% (5.00 to 3.2 to 4.4). Accepted length barely moves (3.29 vs 3.20). On a cache hit, DeepInfer recomputes only the last 128 tokens of sliding-window attention state. That makes recomputation cost constant, regardless of context length. In the decoder layers, DeepSeek says this nearly halves total prefill compute. CPU batch scheduling overlaps with GPU execution, so the GPU never idles between steps. Batch-invariant inference and deterministic sampling are available on NVIDIA only. Structured outputs support regex, JSON schema and EBNF grammars. DeepSeek publishes Pareto curves for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash at 131,072 context. Prefill ran on 4 SM100 GPUs; decode ran on 64. Figures below are read from those charts and are self-reported. DSpark’s dynamic verification adds 4% to 7% throughput at about 60 sequences per rank. At 16 sequences per rank it is 1.5% slower than fixed 5-token verification. A full service still needs a KV cache system and VE/Prefill/Decode disaggregation. It also needs load balancing across data-parallel replicas. DeepSeek team states that those components are tightly coupled to internal infrastructure. Hardware is narrow. Builds require Linux, GCC 13 or later, Python 3.12, and CUDA 13 or CANN 9.2. The smallest efficient production unit is 64 prefill GPUs plus 64 decode GPUs. The internal FlashMLA decoding kernel is 5% to 10% faster than the public one. End-to-end, DeepSeek puts the gap at 5% or less. Check out the GitHub repo , deployment Q&A , deepseek-recipe and the model card . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. title: Exa 3.0 Search API Tops Perplexity, Brave and Parallel on 8 Benchmarks
abstract: Exa has released Exa 3.0 , an upgrade to its web search API for AI agents. The Exa 3.0 search API ships a larger embedding model and a cheaper search type, Exa Lite. Dynamic Highlights is now generally available. Exa claims that it leads Perplexity, Brave and Parallel on 8 benchmarks. Those benchmarks were run by Exa, so you can treat them as self-reported. For developers, the practical change is cost: Lite costs $4 per 1,000 requests . Exa 3.0 is a search API release from Exa Labs that upgrades retrieval quality across every search type. It is available through the API. Exa runs its own crawler and an independent index. It is not a wrapper on Google or Bing results. Exa attributes the gains to 3 changes in its retrieval stack: According to the Exa’s post, Dynamic Highlights uses 95% fewer tokens than full page text while improving answer quality. Highlights carry no extra charge. That matters for agents, where context tokens often cost more than search calls. Exa Lite is a new search type, set with type: "lite" on the /search endpoint, per the changelog . It runs on the same index as Exa Auto. Auto spends more compute on candidate generation, highlights and ranking. Lite supports query, result count, highlights, text, categories, domain and date filters, location and moderation. Unsupported parameters return a 400 error naming the field. Exa now recommends 3 search types: lite , auto and deep . The fast , instant and deep-reasoning types are legacy but still work. Exa compared each provider’s highest-scoring single-step endpoint: Exa 3.0 Auto, Perplexity Web, Brave LLM Context and Parallel Advanced. All ran in one agentic harness. The agent was GPT-6 Luna, with up to 25 search rounds and 10 results per search. Evaluation happened in October 2026. The margins vary widely. ATLAS and WebCode show the clearest leads, at 4.8 and 5.6 points over Perplexity. BrowseComp, DSQA and WideSearch leads are each under 1.5 points over the runner-up. ATLAS is a benchmark Exa published itself on October 8, 2026. On cost, Exa plots agentic search score against cost per task. Lite scores about 79 at about $0.045 per task. Auto scores about 80.5 at about $0.065. Exa says the pair sets a new Pareto frontier among tested providers. All benchmark scores come from Exa’s Exa 3.0 post and were run by Exa. No vendor has published matching results. Prices come from each vendor’s own pricing page. Exa states that it prioritized personal AI assistant use cases. The official technical page lists 1.27B ecommerce listings with prices and availability, and 211M+ local businesses . It also adds real-time news, sports, weather and market data, along with flights, events, transit and podcasts. The Exa Library structures this data into searchable collections. These include 320M people pages, 33M company pages and 500M research paper pages. It also lists 19M SEC filings, 10M patents and 9M court opinions. Check out the Exa 3.0 announcement , the Exa Library , the changelog and the API docs . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. title: Cloudflare Releases Clairic, a System One Extraction Model on Workers AI
abstract: Cloudflare has released a preview of Clairic , a new System One extraction model on Workers AI. The Cloudflare Clairic extraction model reads text or images and returns typed values, not generated text. It targets a job developers usually give to LLMs: pulling totals, dates and IDs into JSON. Clairic answers every requested field in 1 forward pass, with no reasoning and no output tokens. Clairic is a Cloudflare model that extracts, computes, estimates and forecasts typed values from unstructured inputs. It builds on the System One idea from TypeSafe’s Jev , named for Kahneman’s fast, intuitive thinking. Jev and Cloudflare’s own Clef are decision models. They score options you list in advance. Clairic covers answers you cannot list, such as an invoice total, a date or a repair cost. Cloudflare frames a 3-part stack. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values. Decision models turn values into decisions. LLMs turn decisions into words. A request has a state (text plus up to 4 images) and a map of named, typed fields . Each field can carry plain-language instructions. Supported types are text, number, date, time, datetime, duration, list, estimate and forecast, per the Workers AI changelog . Every scalar answer includes p_null , the probability that the value is absent, plus a confidence score. Text answers return exact spans with character offsets. Estimates and forecasts return a median and an 80% interval, from p10 to p90. Forecasts cover up to 64 steps. There is no field limit. Fields that do not fit beside the input in one 8,192-token pass split into parallel passes. Each pass sees the whole input. In the docs example, a 61-token invoice ran in 3 passes. It billed 655 input tokens, including 472 schema tokens. Wide schemas can cost more than the document itself. In a support-email example, Clairic added price and tax into $701.10. It also computed 11 days since delivery. Neither number appears in the email. A missing tracking number returned null instead of a plausible guess. On a skewed receipt photo, it read all 7 present values and returned null for the absent discount. Its lowest confidence was 0.776, on the order number. For forecasting, Cloudflare predicted daily TSA checkpoint counts for 21 days. Average error was 3.3%. 17 of 21 actual counts fell inside the 80% interval. 3 of the 4 misses fell on Columbus Day weekend. The main test is a damaged-product claims pipeline. Clairic extracted facts, Clef chose refund or repair, and GLM-5.3 wrote the reply. Cloudflare compared this against GLM-5.3 handling all 3 steps. The cascade finished in 19.3 s versus 61.7 s, about 3.2x faster. Extraction took 0.46 s against 16.1 s. The decision step took 0.22 s against 21.9 s. Cost per million claims fell 49%, from $11,740 to $6,032. The reply step still dominated, at 18.6 of the 19.3 s. Both pipelines got the facts and decision right. Clairic’s repair estimate was identical across runs. GLM-5.3 returned $250, $250 and $220. Cloudflare says Gemma 4 and Qwen failed the all-LLM version. Clairic is live as a preview at @cf/cloudflare/clairic . Call it through the Workers AI binding with env.AI.run() or the REST API. AI Gateway works with the same endpoints. Pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens with no output charge. That undercuts Clef’s $0.24 but sits above Jev’s $0.042. Weights are promised but not yet released. Check out the Cloudflare blog post , the Clairic model docs , the extraction models explainer and the Workers AI changelog . Also read our earlier coverage of Drex 1.5 . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . title: Inception Releases Mercury 3 Diffusion LLM at 1,068 Tokens per Second
abstract: Inception has released Mercury 3 , the newest version of its diffusion language model. Mercury 3 is a diffusion LLM from Inception that writes answers in parallel, not token by token. Inception reports 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs and a 1M-token context window. On Inception’s own benchmark table, it leads GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on 8 of 12 tests. For developers building agents, voice bots and search tools, this is a speed-first model with competitive scores. Mercury 3 is Inception’s fourth Mercury release, after Mercury 1, Mercury 2 and Mercury 2.5. Mercury 1 launched in 2025. Mercury 2.5 added tunable reasoning and a 260K context window, per Inception’s launch announcement . 1/4 Today, we’re releasing Mercury 3. Mercury 3 is by far our most powerful model and the most intelligent diffusion LLM ever released. It outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Haiku 5.5 on quality while running at 1000+ tok/sec. pic.twitter.com/TYevDl43Lm Autoregressive models write one token after another. Each new token waits for the previous one. A diffusion LLM starts from a rough draft of the full answer. It then refines every position over a few passes in parallel. Fewer sequential steps means faster output on the same GPUs. The open question was whether this approach holds up as models grow larger. Here Inception’s answer is yes. Mercury 3 has more than 40x the total parameters of Mercury 1 (mini). Average quality across standard benchmarks rose about 3x between those 2 models. Speed stayed above 1,000 tokens per second. Inception team plots this as a quality vs size curve across 5 Mercury generations. All scores below come from Inception’s table . Every model ran at medium settings. Mercury 3 posts its largest gains on instruction following and agentic coding. IFBench reaches 76.84, 15 points above GPT-6 Luna. SWE-Bench Atlas reaches 51.08, against 33.33 for Luna and 32.26 for Haiku 5.5. GPQA Diamond lands at 89.23. The losses matter too. Haiku 5.5 wins DeepSWE v1 (51.62 vs 46.31) and MRCR v2 (78.40 vs 75.50). GPT-6 Luna edges ahead on AA-Omniscience-Public (46.94 vs 46.44) and AA-LCR v1.1 (78.30 vs 77.67). Long-context retrieval and longer coding tasks remain the weak spots. Speed and benchmark rows: Inception’s table, medium settings. Specs and prices: each vendor’s own docs. Inception quotes 4 early-access partners. These are customer statements, not independent evals. Mercury 3 is live on the Inception API Platform , OpenRouter , Baseten and Vercel. The API is OpenAI compatible. The docs use the model string mercury-3 and a reasoning_effort parameter. List pricing is $0.20 per 1M input and $0.70 per 1M output tokens. At launch it is 50% off: $0.10 and $0.35. Cached input is 90% off. New accounts get 100M free tokens. Enterprise plans add dedicated capacity, autoscaling and configurable data retention. Inception also ships 2 siblings : Check out the official launch blog , the API docs and the OpenRouter listing . Also read our earlier coverage of Drex 1.5 . title: Meet Drex Max: Nace AI’s Multimodal Decision Model for Computer-Use Agents with a Score 67.59
abstract: Nace AI has released Drex Max , a multimodal decision model for agents that use computers and browsers. The Drex Max multimodal decision model reads text and images and returns calibrated probabilities. It writes no text. Nace team reports 67.59 on the public Decision Index 0.3.2 , 6.9 points above TypeSafe’s Jev 1.14. For agent builders, that means one cheap, typed call per click. Drex Max is a decision model from Nace AI that answers typed questions about text and images. It is the most accurate model in the Drex family , and the only one that reads images. A decision model does not generate tokens. You send a state and named questions. Each question is one of 3 types: noul (yes/no), choice (pick a label) or score (ordered scale). The model returns a probability distribution for each answer in 1 HTTP call. Drex can only answer with the options you gave it. Drex Max uses the same POST /v1/systemone endpoint as every Drex model. You select it with "model": "drex-max" . It is a pinned ID, so drex-latest does not route to it. Images go in an images array. Every question sees the same images, before the state and questions. You refer to them as ‘Image 1’ and ‘Image 2’ in plain text. Each entry is either an uploaded workspace file or inline base64. All scores below come from Nace’s Drex page . They are self-reported. Nace says Drex trains on the index’s official training splits and is scored on held-out splits. Nace lists a 174 ms median per screenshot decision . Jev 1.14 takes 253 ms on the same 243 questions. Nace says Drex Max accepts every screenshot size, while Jev 1.14 rejects 15.9% by size. Across its benchmark table, Nace reports a 183 ms median latency. The launch post cites 34 ms per decision and under 1 second at 262K tokens. Those figures use different setups, so treat them as separate claims. Pricing is $0.06 per 1M input tokens . Output tokens are not billed. New accounts get $25 in signup credit , and failed requests cost nothing. Note: d3-flash’s vision figure is its own evaluation on the 0.3.2 vision board. Drex Max’s figure is Nace’s own run. Cross-vendor numbers are not a controlled comparison. Check out the Drex Max guide , the Drex product page and the launch post . Also read our earlier coverage of Drex 1.5 . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. title: The Roadmap to Becoming an AI Product Manager in 2026
abstract: The Roadmap to Becoming an AI Product Manager in 2026 A structured four-phase roadmap for building the technical fluency, evaluation skills, and governance literacy needed to succeed as an AI product manager in 2026. By Vinod Chugani on October 20, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence AI is reshaping how products are built, shipped, and measured. Companies are finding that the gap between a promising AI prototype and a product users actually trust isn't a research problem. It's a product problem. That gap is where the AI product manager (PM) lives. Unlike traditional product managers who oversee deterministic systems, AI PMs have to navigate outputs that shift, hallucinate, and behave differently across user populations. The role requires fluency in machine learning trade-offs, evaluation systems, compute economics, and regulatory exposure — all while communicating clearly with engineers, lawyers, and executives. This roadmap breaks the path into four phases, moving from technical fluency through to organizational leadership. Each phase builds directly on the last, and the skills compound quickly once the foundational mindset shift takes hold. Step 1: Developing Technical Fluency and the Probabilistic Mindset The first shift every aspiring AI PM needs to make is from deterministic thinking to probabilistic thinking. Traditional software behaves predictably: given input A, you get output B. AI systems produce outputs that are likely , approximate , and context-dependent . That's not a flaw to work around; it's the terrain you're managing. Start by building intuition around the major architecture choices you'll encounter: Foundation model APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini) offer rapid deployment but limited control and ongoing inference costs. Fine-tuning with LoRA or PEFT allows adaptation of open-weight models to domain-specific tasks at lower inference cost. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds model outputs in verified documents, reducing hallucination risk. Small language models (SLMs) running locally are increasingly competitive for latency-sensitive or privacy-constrained use cases. You don't need to implement these architectures. You do need to understand the trade-offs well enough to ask the right questions during scoping and push back on engineering assumptions during planning. At this stage, focus equally on three core tensions you'll manage throughout your career: latency vs. cost vs. accuracy. Token consumption, time-to-first-token (TTFT), and context-window sizing will come up in nearly every product discussion you have. Recommended resources: Hands-On Large Language Models by Jay Alammar and Maarten Grootendorst; the fast.ai Practical Deep Learning course for building architecture intuition without heavy math prerequisites. Portfolio exercise: Build a simple comparison matrix for three different architecture choices applied to a single business problem (for example, customer support automation). Document your trade-off reasoning in writing. Step 2: AI Opportunity Discovery and Feasibility Scoping Once you have the technical vocabulary, the next skill is identifying which AI opportunities are actually worth building — and why most of them aren't. The AI Product Canvas is a structured framework for mapping tasks along two axes: the value if the system performs well, and the risk if it doesn't. High-leverage, low-risk tasks (classification, summarization, document extraction) make solid early candidates. High-risk tasks involving safety, compliance, or irreversible actions need substantially more evaluation infrastructure before they're ready to ship. A critical skill at this phase is the build vs. buy vs. assemble decision: When does consuming a commercial API make sense? When do open-weight models offer a better margin profile? When does a specialized vertical software vendor (for legal, medical, or financial use cases) outcompete both? This decision is partly technical and partly financial. You'll need to model the unit economics of compute : how does your gross margin hold up as token consumption scales? How do GPU hosting costs compare to per-call API fees at 10x your current volume? What does a vector database query cost, and how does that interact with retrieval depth? Getting comfortable with cost modeling at the inference layer is what separates AI PMs who ship sustainable products from those who build impressive demos that collapse under load. Recommended resources: Continuous Discovery Habits by Teresa Torres for opportunity framing; the a16z AI Canon for market context; Anthropic's and OpenAI's public pricing documentation for building cost intuition. Portfolio exercise: Write a one-page build vs. buy recommendation for a specific AI use case in an industry you're familiar with. Include a simple token cost projection. Step 3: AI User Experience, Evaluation Systems, and Iteration This phase is where AI product management diverges most sharply from conventional PM practice. When your product's outputs are probabilistic, you can't rely on binary pass/fail testing. You need an evaluation infrastructure. User experience design for non-deterministic interfaces introduces challenges that don't exist in traditional software. How do you communicate uncertainty to users without eroding trust? How do you design graceful degradation states for when the model is wrong? Where do you insert human-in-the-loop (HITL) checkpoints, and how do you collect feedback signals — explicit ratings, implicit behavioral signals — that actually improve the system over time? On the evaluation side, you need to develop fluency with eval-driven development : Define a "golden dataset" of known inputs and expected outputs before you start iterating. Establish baseline benchmarks early so you can detect regressions. Understand when to use automated metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, precision/recall) and when LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines provide better signal. Map model-level metrics to business KPIs. A 3% improvement in ROUGE score means nothing unless you can explain what it does to resolution rate, escalation rate, or user retention. Red-teaming is not optional. Before launching any user-facing AI feature, run structured adversarial testing — including prompt injection attempts, boundary probing, and worst-case scenario simulation. Build this into your pre-launch checklist from the start, not as an afterthought. Recommended resources: Designing Machine Learning Systems by Chip Huyen; RAGAS documentation for RAG evaluation pipelines; Braintrust and PromptFoo for eval infrastructure. Portfolio exercise: Design an evaluation rubric for a specific AI product feature. Include at least three automated metrics and a description of how you'd run a human evaluation. Step 4: AI Governance, Compliance, and Organizational Leadership The final phase shifts from building to scaling — and from individual contribution to organizational influence. AI products operating at scale face regulatory, legal, and cultural challenges that require the PM to act as a translator between technical, legal, and business stakeholders. Regulatory literacy is becoming non-negotiable. The EU AI Act, U.S. executive orders on AI, sector-specific regulations in healthcare and finance, and data residency laws across jurisdictions will affect what you can build, where you can deploy it, and what documentation you need to maintain. You don't need to become a lawyer, but you need to know enough to flag exposure early and work productively with legal counsel. Data lineage and privacy are ongoing operational concerns. Which customer data is being sent to external model providers? What sanitization pipelines exist before data touches a model? What are your opt-out policies? In enterprise environments, SOC 2 and HIPAA compliance requirements will shape your architecture decisions significantly.

title: 5 Docker Containers for Devs
abstract: 5 Docker Containers for Devs Five self-hosted Docker containers replace the public utility sites where developer data quietly leaks. Learn which ones handle JWT decoding, data transformation, file conversion, API testing, and diagram rendering locally. By Nahla Davies , KDnuggets on October 20, 2026 in Programming The task is small. A JWT needs decoding, a log field is Base64 inside gzip inside hex, or a client sent a HEIC screenshot and the ticket wants a PNG. The fastest route is the third search result, a utility site with a paste box and an ad banner. That is where the token, the log line, and the screenshot end up. Nobody planned to hand internal data to a stranger's web server. It happened because the alternative was fifteen minutes of setup for a five-second job. Five containers close that gap. Each one is a small local service that does a recurring developer chore on your own machine: inspect, transform, convert, test, and diagram. None of them is AI infrastructure, and none overlaps with the agentic developer containers KDnuggets covered earlier. Boring utilities are the point here. Container Use It For Local Advantage First Caution IT-Tools Inspect: JSON, JWT, Base64, hashes, UUIDs, regex, cron One local app instead of a trail of utility tabs Convenience layer, not a secret store or a test suite CyberChef Transform: chained decode, decompress, hash, re-encode Saved recipes make the chain repeatable and shareable Decodes the bytes; does not vouch for what they contain ConvertX Convert: images, documents, e-books, SVG, video, 1,000+ formats Files never leave the machine; accounts and auto-delete built in Untrusted files stay untrusted; claim the first account at once Hoppscotch CE Test: requests, collections, environments, request history Workspace lives next to the project, not in a browser profile Three services plus Postgres; .env and history hold secrets Kroki Diagram: PlantUML, GraphViz, D2, Structurizr and more from text Diagrams as code, rendered with no hosted service Add companion images only for syntaxes a project actually uses The five containers, the chore each one takes over, why it belongs on your machine, and the first thing to watch. Alt text: four-column reference table listing IT-Tools, CyberChef, ConvertX, Hoppscotch CE, and Kroki with the job each one does, its local advantage, and its first caution. Credit: original reference table from the IT-Tools, CyberChef, and ConvertX repositories and the Hoppscotch and Kroki documentation. 1. IT-Tools: The Everyday Dev Toolbox IT-Tools is a single web app holding the small utilities developers otherwise search for one at a time: JSON formatting and comparison, JWT decoding, Base64 in both directions, hash generation, UUIDs, regex testing, cron expression helpers, and color and date converters. The self-host route is one command: docker run -d --name it-tools --restart unless-stopped -p 8080:80 corentinth/it-tools:latest Open localhost:8080 and the whole grab bag is there, on a machine you control — and that is the entire pitch. Nothing about IT-Tools is clever, and it doesn't need to be, because the problem it fixes is a browser history full of decoder sites. Treat it as a convenience layer, though. Nothing you paste into it is stored with any care, so it is not a vault for secrets, and decoding a token there tells you what the token says about itself, not whether your server would accept it. 2. CyberChef: The Data Transformation Bench Some blobs need more than one operation. A log field arrives as hex, which decodes to gzip, which decompresses to JSON with a UTF-16 string inside. CyberChef , built by GCHQ, exists for exactly this chain. You drag operations into a recipe — Base64 and XOR at the simple end, AES and character-set conversion further along — and the recipe re-runs every time the input changes. GCHQ publishes a ready image, ghcr.io/gchq/cyberchef:latest , which serves the app on port 8080 . The recipe, not any single operation, is what you keep. From Hex , then Gunzip , then Decode text as UTF-16, then JSON Beautify is a four-step sequence that can be saved, reloaded, and shared as a URL. The next person who meets the same field then runs the same steps. Breakpoints pause the chain between operations so the intermediate bytes can be inspected, and the Magic operation guesses at nested encodings when the input is a mystery. The app is entirely client-side, which is why it runs in a container with no backend at all. If the blob came from an incident, a customer file, or an internal token, do you want it in an unknown site's paste box? Running CyberChef locally makes that question go away, though it does not vouch for the data. A successful decode shows what the bytes contain, not whether the content is true, complete, or safe to act on. 3. ConvertX: The File Converter You Control File conversion is the clearest case for pulling a utility off the public web, because files carry more than the thing you wanted converted. ConvertX doesn't convert anything itself. It puts one upload page in front of tools you have probably installed and forgotten: FFmpeg for video, ImageMagick for images, LibreOffice and Pandoc for documents, Calibre for e-books, Inkscape for vectors — and the README counts more than a thousand formats between them. The documented deployment is a short Compose file: the ghcr.io/c4illin/convertx image on port 3000 , a JWT_SECRET value, and /app/data mounted to a local folder. The data mount is what lets uploads and results survive a restart. Accounts and password protection come with it, and the default cleanup job removes converted files after 24 hours — which is the right default for a tool that sees screenshots of other people's bugs. The jobs it takes over are the ones that never quite justify a proper tool. A HEIC screenshot has to become a PNG before the bug tracker will accept it. Someone's spec arrived as DOCX and the docs live in Markdown. The ticket system wants the screen recording in a format it recognizes. Not one of those files ever leaves the machine. One honest caveat: local does not mean safe. The converters inside ConvertX parse whatever they are fed, so an untrusted file is still an untrusted file, and the service should stay on localhost or behind real authentication. The README is explicit about the first-run window too. Anyone who reaches the page before you create the first account can register it, so create yours immediately and leave ACCOUNT_REGISTRATION at its default of off. 4. Hoppscotch: The API Tester That Lives With the Project Hoppscotch is an API workspace: requests, collections, environments, and variables, with a history that persists between sessions. The hosted version is fine for a one-off call. Running the Community Edition locally makes sense when API work repeats, because the collections and environments then live next to the project rather than in someone's browser profile. Budget an afternoon for the setup, because this is the heavy one. Hoppscotch CE wants a Postgres database you provide, then either three containers (frontend on 3000 , backend on 3170 , admin on 3100 ) or the all-in-one image that bundles them. Before anything starts you write a .env with the DATABASE_URL , a 32-character DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEY , and the origins allowed to talk to the app, and the first login only works after the Prisma migration has run against that database. Hoppscotch CE is a small stack rather than a toy container. The decision rule is simple: if you test one endpoint once, use the hosted app or curl . If the same API gets exercised every week, the local workspace pays for its setup. Either way, the environment file and the request history contain credentials and internal hostnames, so they get the same handling as any other project secret. 5. Kroki: Diagrams as a Local Service Kroki turns text into diagrams over HTTP.

title: How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins
abstract: Summary: As part of our work experimenting with how Claude can help accelerate drug discovery, we asked an internal research model to design minibinders (small proteins that attach tightly to a target) against scorpion neurotoxins. Claude worked from our prompt and four follow-ups, which we developed in collaboration with the financial investment research firm Citrini Research. Teams at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience experimentally tested 211 designs for binding. Of these, 17 met our criteria. We’re releasing all 211 designs and their data as a resource for the field. In August, we showed how Claude designed protein minibinders after being given a single prompt. A month before we released those results, a team from Citrini Research had approached us with an interesting question: could Claude (and AI drug discovery more generally) enable a group of motivated nonexperts to tackle a genuine problem in human health? Members of our life science research team set out to answer this, first by brainstorming problems with Claude. We landed on asking for Claude’s help designing novel protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins, with the hope that they could one day be used to develop a scorpion antivenom. Scorpions sting 1.2 million people or more every year, resulting in more than 3,250 deaths, mostly among children in parts of the world with limited access to medical care. New treatments are expensive to make, and are also unlikely to earn back the cost of developing them. With so little investment, scorpion envenomation has been described as a neglected tropical disease.
