We started by giving Claude the same prompt we’d used in our earlier protein-binder study, after modifying it with Citrini. 1 Over the next 64 hours, an internal research model, operating within Claude Science, worked mainly autonomously, although we directed its work with four follow-ups. Under our supervision, Claude analyzed the research data, generated the figures, and drafted the final report. Claude’s design campaign produced 17 protein binders that each bind to one of four scorpion neurotoxins that are known to be dangerous to humans. Throughout the process, Claude generated 318,484 protein designs and selected 180 of them for testing. Our team added 31 more, with Claude’s help. Our partners at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, two contract research organizations (CROs), lab-tested all 211 designs to see if they would bind to the toxins they were designed against, and 17 designs met our criteria for a binder. We have not confirmed whether these binders neutralize scorpion venom in a cellular environment, so we do not claim to have produced an antivenom. We sent Claude’s work to two outside experts, Susana Vázquez Torres and Timothy P. Jenkins, who said they felt this work was a promising first step. If AI can now design credible binders against several hard-to-target toxins in days and they can be confirmed in the lab within weeks, this could, in theory, speed up discovery for envenomation and other neglected diseases. The challenge, as always, is turning those binders into safe, affordable, and widely accessible drugs. We share more detail in our technical report , and are making all 211 designs and their data available . Designing a binder against almost any target no longer seems unrealistic. We can now obtain very tight binders remarkably quickly, and binding itself is no longer the main bottleneck. For venomous animals such as snakes and scorpions, whose bites and stings kill or seriously injure large numbers of people, particularly in underserved regions, the real impact will come from tackling the parts of the therapeutic pipeline that go beyond binding. The challenge is to use these extraordinary tools to develop molecules that can become real drugs, ones that are safe, affordable, and widely accessible. Susana Vázquez Torres , Postdoctoral Researcher, Structural Biology Programme, Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO), Madrid, Spain. Designing de novo binders against five toxins from four species of scorpions Scorpion venom contains multiple protein neurotoxins. The neurotoxins that are most likely to harm or kill humans attach to sodium channels , large proteins embedded in the membranes of nerve cells that allow them to fire. When sodium channels are disrupted, nerves fire at the wrong time—this releases large amounts of stress chemicals, like adrenaline. In severe cases, this can cause heart failure and excess fluid buildup in the lungs, occasionally resulting in death. There are some antivenoms available for scorpion stings. They’re generally made using the antibodies of immunized animals, a process that can take months. Venom is milked from thousands of scorpions and used to immunize horses; scientists then purify the resulting antibodies from the horses’ blood. Traditional antivenoms can work when given early, but they’re usually effective for only a small number of neurotoxins. They’re also expensive to produce, and in many regions are costly or in short supply. De novo design offers a potential solution. A binder is a molecule that attaches tightly to a specific target; antibodies are one natural example. In principle, a binder that targets the part of a neurotoxin that latches onto sodium channels could stop the toxin from reaching the channel. In de novo design, protein binders are generated from scratch against a specific target. These binders are designed computationally and can be optimized for druglike properties such as potency and stability, which could make them easier to supply in regions where stings most often occur. Our approach was inspired by an earlier effort that designed de novo proteins that neutralized snake neurotoxins and protected mice. To our knowledge, no de novo -designed binders against scorpion neurotoxins have been described. For this campaign, we chose to target five scorpion-venom neurotoxins across four regions: Mexico (Cn2), Brazil (Ts1), North Africa (AaH I and AaH II), and the Middle East (LqhIII). We also chose to aim the designs at each toxin’s channel-binding site. Claude picked the toxin structures to use for design by searching the Protein Data Bank (PDB) as well as the AlphaFold database (AFDB). For each toxin, it selected five hotspots , specific amino acid positions on the toxin that its binder designs were meant to latch onto. We were primarily wondering if Claude could design binders against individual toxins. But we were also curious if Claude could design binders that targeted multiple toxins. There’s a practical reason for trying to design multitoxin binders, namely that it would reduce the number of molecules needed for a universal antivenom cocktail—which would be the most cost-effective and regionally neutral treatment. We selected these five scorpion toxins (Cn2, Ts1, AaH I, AaH II, and LqhIII) as a challenging test of multitoxin design: they share one fold for the overall shape of the protein, but any two are only 26% to 62% identical in their amino acid sequences. To see how far Claude could go, we asked it to design four kinds of binders: binders against each of the five toxins individually; binders that targeted the β-family toxins Ts1 and Cn2; binders that targeted the α-family toxins AaH II, AaH I, and LqhIII; and binders that targeted all five toxins simultaneously. Designing credible binders against five toxins in parallel, in a matter of days, is a great showcase of the AI-driven paradigm shift we are seeing in therapeutic discovery. This is especially true for neglected diseases such as animal envenomings, which have been largely starved of innovation due to low commercial incentives. Being able to agentically tackle the uniquely broad target space across animal toxins provides a significant speed-up in discovery, and brings realistic therapeutic solutions much closer. Timothy P. Jenkins , Associate Professor, Technical University of Denmark.

title: Work management context for AI agents with Smartsheet MCP on AWS
abstract: AI agents are most useful when they can act on the real work happening across your organization. Work management involves complex, cross-functional tasks such as updating project timelines, reassigning tasks, and surfacing status. AI agents can support you with these without anyone switching tools. Smartsheet , the work management platform for managing projects, portfolios, and operations, has launched a generally available Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server. With the Smartsheet MCP Server , AI assistants can read, write, and manage Smartsheet data through a standardized protocol. The protocol spans more than 40 tools for exploring, creating, and managing sheets, rows, columns, and automations. You can update task statuses, create rows, and modify project structure directly through natural language. In this post, we walk through two ways you can connect it to your existing workflows. Amazon Quick is an agentic AI workspace built for business users, project managers, and operations teams. They can ask questions, update sheets, and build dashboards through natural language without writing code. Kiro is an agentic IDE where developers connect to Smartsheet through MCP to reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow. The following diagram shows how the Smartsheet MCP Server sits as the central integration layer connecting to AWS services. Amazon Quick and Kiro connect directly as MCP clients. Amazon Quick serves knowledge workers, project managers, and operations teams who want to query, update, and automate Smartsheet through natural language. With Kiro, developers can reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow. The following architecture diagram illustrates these integration paths: the Smartsheet MCP Server in the center, with Amazon Quick and Kiro as MCP clients on the left, and Smartsheet’s API and data layer on the right. Figure 1: Smartsheet MCP Server architecture showing MCP client connections from Amazon Quick and Kiro through the server to the Smartsheet API layer Consider a software engineering team that tracks their sprint in Smartsheet. Tasks, owners, statuses, and blockers all live in a project sheet. Here’s what each path looks like for the same team: When a user such as a project manager wants to check which sprint tasks are blocked this week, they can ask Amazon Quick through natural language. The Amazon Quick chat agent queries the Smartsheet MCP Server, pulls the relevant rows, and surfaces a summary with owner names and due dates. The response is generated from live Smartsheet data without building a report or dashboard. For developers who are fixing bugs or working through features, they can ask Kiro to pull the current sprint sheet and show them the open backend tasks assigned to them. Kiro queries Smartsheet through MCP and surfaces the list inline. When the fix is committed, a Kiro hook automatically updates the corresponding row status to Complete. Smartsheet MCP Server delivers precisely structured context, including row relationships, column types, cell history, and comments. This produces token-efficient payload sizes rather than returning raw API payloads. This engineering decision compounds into reduced cost and improved latency at scale when running hundreds of AI-assisted queries across a project portfolio. To learn how Smartsheet built their remote MCP server on AWS, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS . Before connecting the Smartsheet MCP Server to Amazon Quick and Kiro, verify that you have the following in place: The Smartsheet MCP Server is available at three regional endpoints. It uses Streamable HTTP transport (MCP spec versions 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26) and is authenticated with either OAuth 2.0 or a Personal Access Token. Both options expose the same Smartsheet toolset. The right choice depends on where your work gets done: Choose Amazon Quick if you need a fully managed, organization-wide solution your whole team can use: no app registration, only pre-built OAuth, and it scales across knowledge workers in your enterprise. Choose Kiro if you’re a developer who wants something lightweight: no infrastructure, only a config file and a personal access token, scoped to your own workflow. Amazon Quick includes Smartsheet as a pre-built connector in its directory. That means reading project status, updating rows, creating discussions, and surfacing risks, all in the same interface your business users already work in. Amazon Quick makes that integration available across the organization, from project managers and operations teams to business users who manage work in Smartsheet. Figure 2: The Smartsheet connector in the Amazon Quick Connectors directory Figure 3: Entering the Smartsheet connection details in Amazon Quick Figure 4: The Manage Tools and Permissions page for the Smartsheet connector Figure 5: Choosing who can access the Smartsheet connection on the Publish page After you’re connected, your Amazon Quick chat agent can work with Smartsheet data through natural language: Figure 6: Amazon Quick chat response summarizing overdue tasks from a Smartsheet project sheet with key observations and recommended actions Kiro is the right path when developers want Smartsheet project context available directly in their development environment, alongside their code, without context-switching. Kiro is built around spec-driven development. It turns high-level prompts into structured specs, then into working code, docs, and tests. MCP servers are how Kiro gets real-world context by connecting to documentation, databases, APIs, and enterprise systems to ground its agent in live data rather than training-time knowledge. A Kiro feature called powers is a one-click installable bundle that packages a curated MCP server with steering files and hooks. It gives the Kiro coding agent a new capability out of the box. For Smartsheet, configuring the connection takes a single JSON configuration block and from that point, the Kiro agent can reference live project data as part of a development workflow. To connect the Smartsheet MCP Server to Kiro, add it to your Kiro MCP configuration ( .kiro/settings/mcp.json for workspace scope). For a full walkthrough, see Getting Started with Kiro and MCP Servers : This configuration uses the Personal Access Token (API key) approach. For production deployments, OAuth is recommended. Set SMARTSHEET_API_TOKEN to your Smartsheet Personal Access Token in your environment. Kiro loads MCP servers as background processes on startup. After it’s initialized, Smartsheet tools are available to the Kiro agent across all modes: chat, spec planning, and hooks-based automation. Full details in the Smartsheet MCP Server Documentation . From there, Kiro can reference Smartsheet data as part of development workflows: Figure 7: Kiro generating a prioritized fix list from open bugs in the Backend API project sheet Figure 8: Kiro creating a spec from the in-progress features in the Q3 Roadmap sheet For builders deploying in regulated or enterprise environments, the Smartsheet MCP Server security model is built on the same infrastructure and permissions layer as the Smartsheet REST API. It’s not a new trust boundary: For compliance architects, the MCP Server doesn’t store prompts, and prompt content stays between the AI client and the model. Smartsheet sees only the structured tool calls and their results. If you followed this walkthrough and want to remove the integration afterward, here’s how to undo each path: For background on how the server works, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS . After you’ve connected the Smartsheet MCP Server to your system of choice, here are four actions we recommend trying: You can ask the chat agent to monitor your active project sheets, identify rows marked Blocked or At Risk.

title: From data to decisions: Conversational supply chain intelligence with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Giving supply chain teams direct access to the systems behind their decisions. Every supply chain generates constant signals: orders in approval, shifting lead times, slowing ports, drifting prices, disruptions. The problem isn’t scarce data. It’s the distance between the data and the decision-maker. Answering “which top-revenue SKUs are exposed to the current port closure, and what will it cost?” used to mean knowing which system held each piece and stitching them together by hand while the domain expert waited. Could that manager instead ask in plain language and get an actionable, cross-system answer in seconds? Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the intelligence layer, exposing enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers as a composable tool layer. Amazon Quick turns that into action for personas with no setup. Answers come from live systems of record and grounded documents, not model recall, and every change waits for a named human. In this post, we walk through this pattern end to end, from a conversational walkthrough in Amazon Quick to the AgentCore tool layer behind it, and we show you how to deploy it yourself. Figure 1: Domain expertise sits with users while operational data is fragmented across ERP, monitoring, procurement, and email Each question needs its own tool: inventory from the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, disruptions from email or news, a request for quotation (RFQ) from procurement, and compliance from a checklist. Correlating is manual. A manager’s morning traditionally spans the ERP (inventory exceptions), monitoring tool (alerts), procurement (alternatives), email (RFQ), and a tracker: 45–60 minutes across five systems with a dozen-plus context switches. Conversationally it’s three prompts in one tool, “Any critical disruptions affecting my top-revenue SKUs?” → “Assess the TechComp halt and issue an emergency RFQ to approved alternatives” → “Looks good. Send it.”, in minutes. Figure 2: Traditional multi-tool flow versus a single conversational thread orchestrated by AgentCore The following five steps follow one disruption from detection to an approved emergency RFQ, all in a single Amazon Quick conversation. The user asks “What supply chain tools do I have?” and Amazon Quick lists the supply chain MCP servers published in AWS Agent Registry. Because an administrator has turned on the registry integration, the four business MCP servers already appear as connector cards, with connection details pre-populated and no URLs to enter by hand. The orchestration agent is added as its own MCP connector. “Check active supply disruptions” calls the Disruption Alerts MCP ( assess_disruption_impact ): three disruptions with severity, region, and SKU counts. How we solve it: Quick routes the request through AgentCore to the MCP server, which queries backend monitoring and returns a structured result, no dashboard or export. The user opens the TechComp Production Halt. assess_disruption_impact(disruption_id="DISR-002") correlates order, customer, and inventory data: $750K at risk, 23 orders, three days of supply. How we solve it: one MCP tool call fans out across systems of record, so the manager gets a consolidated impact read without touching the ERP. The user asks for mitigation. recommend_mitigation(disruption_id="DISR-002") chains the Governance MCP (verify approved alternatives) and Quoting MCP (contract-aligned quote), one flow from one request. How we solve it: the agent plans and sequences the calls, so a single ask spans disruption, governance, and quoting with no manual hand-offs. The user then sets up proactive monitoring (“Alert me every morning if there’s a new critical disruption”). The same flow can run unattended from an inbound supplier email. How we solve it: the same agent and tools run on a schedule or email trigger, posting review-ready cards to the Activity Feed for a person to approve. Put end to end, those five steps are a single runtime sequence: Figure 3: Runtime sequence for the walkthrough, where every result returns to Amazon Quick for approval That’s the experience. Here’s how it is built: the pattern separates the intelligence layer from the interface layer, so each evolves independently, with Amazon Quick as the interface and AgentCore as the intelligence. Figure 4: End-to-end architecture from Amazon Quick to AgentCore (Gateways, Runtime, Identity, Policy) to backends, with AWS Agent Registry alongside Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a modular agentic platform for building, deploying, and operating agents securely at scale. It offers more than we use here. Four of its services are relevant to this pattern: MCP is an open standard for how AI models interact with external tools. Each server exposes tools with typed parameters: The registry is the governed discovery layer: a publisher submits a record, a curator approves it, and only then is it discoverable through hybrid search, browsing, or the registry’s MCP endpoint. One scale reality worth noting: because schemas are discovered at runtime, treat each as a contract, versioning new alongside old for breaking changes. Figure 5: Publishing an MCP server record to AWS Agent Registry, a curator approving it, an administrator linking it to Quick, and approved records becoming connector cards The reasoning layer is an agent on AgentCore Runtime, an agent record at its direct invocation URL through a Custom MCP connector, with no Lambda or gateway. Here, it’s the Order Fulfillment Agent. Given one request it plans which tools to call and in what order: Every tool call passes through the same AgentCore control set before it reaches a backend. Figure 6: The uniform AgentCore control set before the backend (IAM auth, per-tool authorization, input validation, policy evaluation, rate limiting, data-boundary enforcement, audit logging) Amazon Quick puts AgentCore tools before business users through chat, agents, the Activity Feed, and automated workflows, with no technical setup. The Activity Feed is the proactive surface of Amazon Quick, a unified inbox where agents post results, alerts, and recommendations. Feed items are: AgentCore tools plus the proactive capabilities of Amazon Quick give two paths, time-based and email-driven, through a common trigger → agent → output pipeline. Figure 7: Three-stage pipeline from trigger (schedule or email) to autonomous agent (assess_disruption_impact, check_supplier_approval, apply_approval_rules, validate_quote) to review-ready card Suppliers reply to an emergency RFQ by email with pricing. The agent validates each (approved supplier? within guidelines?) and stages the result. It does not author a quote, pick a winner, or issue a purchase order (PO). Phase 1: Setup (one-time, approximately 5 minutes) Phase 2: Runtime (fully automated) The feed card carries the validation results and decision-relevant facts: The reviewer compares validated responses and either selects a supplier and issues the PO, or rejects with a logged reason. Selection and the PO stay with a person. Schedule-triggered, the same pattern applies: a daily 8:30 AM agent checks for new critical or high-severity disruptions, assesses impact, flags anything under seven days of supply as URGENT, and posts an alert card with an Issue Emergency RFQ action. This isn’t a “replace everything” argument. Dashboards remain superior for trend visualization, collaborative analysis, regulatory reporting, and exploratory analysis. Use conversational AI for real-time operational decisions and BI for strategic analysis. They complement, not compete. One Quick Agent serves all three personas: the manager maintains continuity, procurement sources with compliance-awareness, the analyst correlates signals. Persona also bounds reach, through row/column-level security and per-persona MCP-tool scoping, so procurement does not see finance data.

title: Fine-tuning GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
abstract: GPT-OSS-20B is an open-weight reasoning model that thinks in English. Ask it to reason in French, German, Spanish, or Italian and it acknowledges the instruction, then produces its chain-of-thought in English anyway. On a 50-example multilingual reasoning test, the base model reasoned in the correct target language only 22 percent of the time. That 22 percent was almost entirely the English examples (English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent). For teams deploying reasoning models for non-English users, that gap matters. A user who asks a question in French expects the model to reason and answer in French, not to switch to English mid-thought. Closing that gap is a fine-tuning problem. It raises a question every team faces once they start customizing open-weight models: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), or both? In this post, we walk through how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod . We show when SFT alone was sufficient and when GRPO added measurable value on top. To understand more broadly when GRPO helps, we also ran a controlled Qwen2.5-7B experiment across two tasks with different capability gaps. The short answer: SFT does most of the work, GRPO refines when there is headroom to refine, and matching the technique to the capability gap is what decides the outcome. This section covers the multilingual reasoning task and dataset, how SFT and GRPO complement each other, and the training stack we ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. The dataset is HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking — a chain-of-thought reasoning dataset translated into French, Spanish, German, and Italian alongside English, roughly 949 training and 50 validation examples. The model receives a reasoning language: system-prompt instruction and must both reason and answer in that target language, overriding its strong English prior. The evaluation is 50 test cases: 10 math/logic problems across 5 languages (EN/FR/DE/ES/IT). The clearest way to think about the two techniques: SFT teaches a behavior the model doesn’t have. GRPO optimizes a behavior the model can already sometimes produce. GRPO works by sampling a group of responses per prompt and pushing the policy toward the above-average ones. If the desired behavior has zero probability in the base distribution, there is very little for GRPO to reinforce. That single idea explains almost every result in this post. We ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) orchestration. For the initial SFT and GRPO runs on GPT-OSS-20B, we used the PyTorch TRL library. For the Qwen control experiment, we switched to veRL as the trainer, with Ray and KubeRay for distributed orchestration and vLLM for fast rollout generation. Checkpoints and datasets lived on Amazon FSx for Lustre, and the inter-node fabric used Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). All fine-tuning used Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which is parameter-efficient and well-suited to both SFT and GRPO. The following diagram shows the training data path end-to-end. A submission from the user lands on the Amazon EKS control plane of the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster. Amazon EKS schedules a Ray head pod plus worker pods that run the veRL trainer and vLLM rollout workers. Both sets of pods mount Amazon FSx for Lustre for the base model, training data, and checkpoints. Inter-node collectives use EFA. Rollouts stream from vLLM back to the veRL trainer, and the trainer writes checkpoints back to Amazon FSx for Lustre. Figure 1: End-to-end training data path for SFT and GRPO fine-tuning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with veRL, Ray, KubeRay, vLLM, and Amazon FSx for Lustre for Qwen control experiments The following describes each hop in more detail. The submitter starts the run from Amazon SageMaker Studio or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). The Amazon EKS control plane on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod places pods on GPU nodes and starts a Ray head with worker pods for the veRL trainer and the vLLM rollout workers. Amazon FSx for Lustre provides shared, high-throughput storage for the base model, the training data, and the checkpoints. When training completes, the trainer writes the LoRA adapter back to Amazon FSx for Lustre for downstream evaluation or serving. All of the commands, manifests, and scripts referenced below live in the awsome-distributed-ai GitHub repository under 3.test_cases/pytorch/trl/gpt-oss-lora-grpo/ . Clone the repository and change into the test case directory: Copy the environment template, then edit env_vars to set your ECR registry, image name, tag, and HuggingFace token: Build the training image and push it to your registry. The image bundles PyTorch, TRL, HuggingFace Transformers, PEFT, and the training and inference scripts: Point kubectl at your cluster and apply the FSx storage manager pod. The storage manager gives you a shell into the shared file system for checkpoint conversion and eval-log inspection: We begin by measuring the base model, then configure the SFT run and examine the results. Base GPT-OSS-20B on the 50-case eval scored 22 percent reasoning-language correct (11/50). Per-language: English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent. The model defaults to English reasoning regardless of the instruction. The SFT setup used LoRA r=8, α=16, trained for 1,000 steps on 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB) with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) full-shard, bf16 precision, and gradient checkpointing. The job runs as an elastic HyperPodPyTorchJob managed by Kueue, launched with hyperpodrun . Loss and gradient norm print each step. A healthy run looks like this: When training completes, convert the FSDP checkpoint to the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) format that TRL’s GRPO trainer and the inference scripts expect: After SFT, the model reasons in the correct language 100 percent of the time (50/50) across all five languages. SFT learned this in two stages: Takeaway: SFT is not optional here. The base model can’t follow the reasoning-language instruction at all, and SFT takes reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent. The remaining gap is answer-language at 62 percent. That’s the harder half, because the final answer is short and the English prior is strongest there. Answer-language was the obvious target for GRPO. SFT already produced correct reasoning 100 percent of the time, and the model sometimes produced the answer in the right language, so there was a signal to reinforce. We ran GRPO with TRL’s GRPOTrainer , starting from the SFT checkpoint. The setup: load the SFT LoRA, call merge_and_unload , and add a new LoRA (r=8, α=16, about 0.068 percent trainable parameters, 13.6M of 20B). Training used K=8 generations per prompt, device_map=auto , learning rate 1e-6, and 10 epochs. The reward function scored answer-language (±5.0), reasoning-language (±1.5), and brevity (+0.5 or −1.0), for a combined range of −7.5 to +7.0. Launch GRPO from the converted SFT checkpoint: GRPO writes checkpoints to /fsx/checkpoints/grpo-singlenode/ . Pick the best checkpoint against your held-out eval (the answer-language metric peaked early in this run) and convert it to PEFT format for inference and evaluation. Result (from the SFT checkpoint): GRPO delivered a real +8 point gain on the answer-language metric while holding reasoning at 100 percent. The gain came where there was headroom to gain. Answer-language was the sometimes-correct behavior that SFT had not fully converged on, and GRPO reinforced it. To see the qualitative difference, deploy three inference pods that share the same base model but load different adapters: Run the same French-reasoning prompt through each variant: The base pod reasons in English despite the instruction. The SFT pod reasons in French but often answers in English.

title: How Octave built a secure multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: In quality management for regulated industries, the institutional memory that resolves a problem is almost always buried somewhere in a customer’s history. A similar defect investigated last year, a Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) that fixed the root cause, an audit finding that flagged the same gap. That knowledge sits in billions of documents no human can search by semantic similarity across languages and formats, so every investigation starts from scratch. Octave Reliance has helped each organization collect documents across multiple systems to help them search more easily and keep track of everything they have. The Octave Reliance team saw unlocking this history as its single largest opportunity to help customers work faster and stay compliant. The obstacle was equally clear: complaint records, audit findings, and corrective actions carry the platform’s strictest isolation requirements, and those were exactly the records the AI would need to read. In a platform serving over 14,000 customers across medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and food manufacturing, a single inadvertent disclosure from one customer to another would carry regulatory consequences far outweighing any AI benefit. Octave operates across 180 countries, serving more than 60% of the Global Fortune 500 . Its cloud-native quality management system, Reliance , supports over 650 enterprise customers with over 40 applications, from complaint management and CAPA tracking to audit management and supplier quality. Everyone generates regulated data that AI could reason over. Each customer is a separate tenant and no data can cross a tenant boundary. Faced with that, the Reliance team made an unusual call: rather than shipping one AI feature, it spent its first cycle building a foundation every future feature would sit on. That foundation has since cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent. If you are bringing AI to a software as a service (SaaS) platform where the data is valuable, but isolation is non-negotiable, the reasoning travels beyond quality management. In this post, we walk through the four tensions that shaped the design and the three-layer foundation Octave built with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock. We then follow the pipeline that embedded 2 billion documents and the Complaint Triage Assistant that proved it in production. Envisioning workshops with AWS surfaced four high-impact use cases: complaint summarization and triage, audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring. They also surfaced the insight that shaped everything after dozens of applications, each with different document types and workflows. Building AI for one in a silo meant rebuilding the infrastructure for the next. So, the team inverted the plan: build the horizontal platform first, then cut vertical feature slices into it. Complaint summarization and triage went first, to prove the architecture before the rest followed. Before selecting a single model, the team spent its time on four problems that pulled in different directions. None could be traded away. Making data available without risking inadvertent disclosure. Complaint records, CAPAs, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and audit findings belong to one tenant and must be unreachable by another. Not even an errant AI query could cross. Vector store, retrieval logic, and generation context all had to be scoped to a single tenant. Executing agents in isolation. The permissions governing an agent’s tools, data stores, and model endpoints had to be scoped to the requesting user rather than a shared service role, available only during execution, and respectful of that user’s access rights. A shared agent pool with static credentials failed all three. Reading content that cannot be trusted. Agents here ingest complaints, email attachments, scanned PDFs, and images from outside the organization. The OWASP Top 10 for large language model (LLM) Applications (2025) names the threats that apply directly: prompt injection through ingested content (LLM01), sensitive information disclosure (LLM02), improper output handling (LLM05), and excessive agency (LLM06). Hidden instructions in an attached PDF are not hypothetical at this volume. Embedding 2 billion documents without a quarter-long wait. Reliance hosts more than 2 billion documents, with individual tenants storing millions of Word files, PDFs, scanned forms, spreadsheets, images, and email. The team committed to onboarding even the largest tenant within a single working day. Because these documents inform regulatory decisions, quality could not be traded for throughput. A missed complaint erodes trust in the whole system. Holding four tensions at once narrowed the options considerably. Amazon Bedrock addressed them as one platform: multi-model access through a single API, the AWS Region residency and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) governance the AWS account already enforces, and Guardrails as production content controls rather than something to build. The foundation resolves into three layers, shown in Figure 1. Data preparation embeds quality documents with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock and writes them to a per-tenant vector store on Amazon OpenSearch Service . Secure execution passes a user request through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , which applies authentication and policy before handing it to an isolated microVM session that calls an Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock. Wrapping both, content protection applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails twice: input filtering on the way in, output filtering before anything reaches the handler. Retrieval, execution, and screening stay in separate stages, so each can be enforced and evidenced on its own. Figure 1: High-level architecture of the Reliance AI foundation Nothing else worked until the documents were retrievable. That meant accurately, across languages and formats, and not across a tenant boundary. The team evaluated embedding models against its own corpus rather than public leaderboards. The deciding questions were specific to this data: what a photo of a cracked housing has to do with the paragraph describing it, and a German complaint with an English CAPA. Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock won on five counts and they weren’t independent of each other. What was decided first was how much of the pipeline was made unnecessary. Quality records carry photos of defective products, scanned inspection forms, and annotated diagrams alongside text. Embed v4 places both modalities in one vector space. A photo of a cracked housing and the paragraph describing that defect are retrievable from a single query, with no separate pipeline per modality. Native multilingual support does the same work along the other axis: documents arrive in multiple languages, often inside one tenant’s corpus, and need no translation preprocessing. Two pipelines the team never had to build, and two fewer places for a document to fall out of retrieval. The remaining three counts settled where the vectors could live and what they would cost. Customer data can’t leave its AWS Region, even for inference, so in-Region model availability on Amazon Bedrock was a precondition rather than a convenience. Embed v4 supports in-Region inference in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1), Europe (Ireland) Region (eu-west-1), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) Region (ap-northeast-1), covering three of Octave’s regional compliance requirements. Model and feature availability varies by Region and changes over time. For current coverage, see Regional availability by models in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Within each Region, Amazon OpenSearch Service costs scale linearly with dimension count. That made Embed v4’s configurable output dimensions of 256–1,536 worth testing rather than accepting by default.

title: Access OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock from Canada with cross-Region inference
abstract: Canadian organizations building generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock often need the latest foundation models (FMs), such as OpenAI GPT-6.1, OpenAI GPT-6, and GPT-5.6, accessible from the Canadian AWS Regions. With Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference (CRIS), you can now access these models from Canada. OpenAI GPT-5.6 models (Sol, Terra, and Luna), GPT-6 (Astra, Sol, and Luna), and GPT-6.1 Sol are available from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions. Inference is processed in North America, with data-residency controls described later in this post. Cross-Region inference is a capacity mechanism. Your application calls the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint in your source Region. Amazon Bedrock then routes the request to a supported destination Region for processing. With this approach, you get access to a broader capacity pool that can help your application sustain throughput during demand spikes. You don’t need to manage destination Region routing in your application. In this post, we walk through the GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 models available from Canada and the cross-Region inference profiles that serve them. We then show how to set up permissions and invoke the models with the OpenAI Responses API, Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. For the Responses API, we include streaming and tool-use examples. Finally, we cover how to request quota increases, review the observability signals available in your source Region, and clean up when you are done. With Amazon Bedrock, you can access three families of OpenAI models in Canada through cross-Region inference. The following table summarizes each model and its positioning. These models accept text and image inputs, return text, and support a 1-million-token context window, reasoning mode, and tool calling. GPT-6.1 Sol supports the same context window and tool calling, with additional input and output modalities documented in its model card. GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 also support prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock (see the Prompt caching section). These models are available through the OpenAI Responses API, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. For pricing, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . For per-model Region availability, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide . Amazon Bedrock inference profiles are logical identifiers you pass in place of a raw model ID. Each profile defines a model and the set of Regions to which Amazon Bedrock can route a request. Two profile types are available from Canada: Endpoint availability differs by model and source Region, as shown in the following table. Profile membership and model availability can change. The global profile for the GPT-5.6 models is available only from ca-central-1 . From ca-west-1 , use the US geographic profile for GPT-5.6. Verify the active profiles for your source Region before deployment, either with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or on the console (see the following section), or see the Cross-Region inference support documentation . The following sections walk through the setup and code needed to invoke these models from your Canadian source Region. Before you begin, confirm that you have the following: For quick exploration, attach the AWS managed policy AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess . For deployed workloads with stricter access controls, use a least-privilege custom policy. The following example grants access to the GPT-6 Astra global profile from ca-central-1 : If you authenticate through the API-key path (bearer token for the OpenAI SDK), also grant bedrock:CallWithBearerToken . For the Responses API, add bedrock:InvokeModel on arn:aws:bedrock:ca-central-1:*:project/default . If your organization restricts Regions through SCPs, use the bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition key to allow CRIS traffic while blocking direct calls to unapproved Regions. The following SCP denies Amazon Bedrock inference outside your approved source Regions unless the request uses a CRIS inference profile: With this condition, Amazon Bedrock can route to the profile’s destination Regions even when those Regions are otherwise denied by your SCP. Every destination Region in your chosen profile must be allowed for the request to succeed. For more detail, see Set up cross-Region inference in multi-account environments . Before invoking a model, you can verify which profiles are active in your source Region with the AWS CLI. The following command lists the active OpenAI profiles from ca-central-1 . To run the same check from Calgary, replace ca-central-1 with ca-west-1 . The Amazon Bedrock console offers the same view. Open the console, choose Canada (Central) or Canada West (Calgary) as your Region, choose Cross-Region inference under Inference , and review the available profiles. The following screenshot shows the active OpenAI inference profiles listed on the Amazon Bedrock console for the Canada (Central) Region. Figure 1: Active OpenAI cross-Region inference profiles on the Amazon Bedrock console (Canada (Central)) GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 support three access paths on the bedrock-runtime endpoint: the OpenAI Responses API, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. The OpenAI-compatible APIs are called on the /openai/v1 paths of the endpoint. The endpoint accepts either AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) or an Amazon Bedrock API key . The following examples use the Amazon Bedrock token generator for Python to create a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key from your current AWS credentials, so your application does not need to store a static key. For applications that already use the OpenAI SDK with the Responses API, point the client at the Regional Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint and pass the inference profile ID as the model. For streaming output, set stream=True and iterate over the response events, printing text as it arrives: The OpenAI Chat Completions format works through the same endpoint. For the full list of supported parameters, including reasoning effort levels, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Use the Converse API when your application calls Amazon Bedrock through an AWS SDK. Boto3 resolves credentials through the standard AWS credential chain. The same call works for GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6.1 Sol by changing the inference profile ID. The following example uses the US geographic profile for GPT-6 Sol and the global profile for GPT-6 Luna. Both were validated from ca-central-1 . These models support client-side tool use (function calling) . Define tools in the tools parameter, and the model returns a structured tool-call request for your application to execute. GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 support prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock to reduce the cost and latency of repeated prompt prefixes. Implicit caching requires no changes to your code: Amazon Bedrock automatically caches eligible prefixes of 1,024 tokens or more. Cached tokens read on subsequent requests are billed at a discounted rate and do not count against your tokens-per-minute quota. Cached tokens appear in the response usage object and in Amazon CloudWatch metrics so you can track usage. For cache-write pricing, minimum prefix sizes, and support for explicit cache breakpoints, see the prompt caching documentation and the individual model cards . Cross-Region inference quotas on the bedrock-runtime endpoint are measured in tokens per minute (TPM) per model. Each quota combines input and output tokens against a single limit. US geographic and global inference profiles have separate quota allocations, so switching between them changes the pool you draw from. Token consumption combines input tokens, cache-write input tokens, and output tokens. Output tokens are multiplied by the model’s burndown rate, so output-heavy workloads consume quota faster than raw token counts suggest.

title: Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry
abstract: Runtime discovery with AWS Agent Registry can help address a problem that agent demos might hide. Hardcoded tools work fine for a handful, start to degrade at a few dozen, and become unmanageable beyond that. Enterprise systems expose hundreds of internal APIs for pricing, support, orders, inventory, and customer data. In these systems, the model can spend more tokens disambiguating tool names than reasoning about the user’s request. Each new capability requires a code change in the orchestrator, a redeploy, and a coordinated release across teams that would much rather ship on their own cadence. This pattern can arise across enterprise software as a service (SaaS) engagements where teams expose large internal API surfaces to agentic consumers. Build-time wiring can become a bottleneck as the catalog expands. One approach is to change how the orchestrator accesses its tools: instead of compiling every tool into the agent, the agent can discover relevant tools at runtime. AWS Agent Registry is a managed service for cataloging and discovering Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agents, and agent skills. Publishers register protocol-specific descriptors and searchable descriptions. At runtime, an orchestrator can search approved, discoverable records and use the returned endpoint and descriptor content to construct a client. Registry search results do not return the capability’s invocation credentials or authentication scheme. This post walks through the Discover → Instantiate → Execute loop demonstrated by the refactored Python sample. The code deploys an order-management MCP server through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, two agent-to-agent (A2A) agents on AgentCore runtime , a Registry, and an orchestrator. The sample directory contains the deployment script, orchestrator, helper modules, and cleanup script. The orchestrator agent in this sample has no built-in knowledge of tools or agents. Figure 1: Without AWS Agent Registry (left), endpoints are hardcoded and adding a new agent means code changes plus redeployment. With AWS Agent Registry (right), the orchestrator discovers capabilities through semantic search and new integrations are usable after registration and approval The orchestrator sends a natural-language query to the AWS Agent Registry data plane. The search response includes record identity, name, description, record type, status, version, and protocol descriptors such as MCP server metadata or an A2A agent card. It does not include invocation credentials. The application must obtain and apply the appropriate credentials through a separate, trusted configuration path. For each returned record, the orchestrator constructs a client from the descriptor type. In this sample, the registered MCP server represents tools that were first added as targets to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. The MCP descriptor therefore points to the Gateway endpoint. The orchestrator fetches a Cognito OAuth access token separately and uses it when creating the MCPClient . A2A records contain an agent card whose URL identifies an AgentCore runtime endpoint. The wrapper invokes that runtime through the boto3 data-plane client, which signs the request with the caller’s AWS credentials. Registry discovery supplies connection metadata, not the authentication material. An ephemeral inner agent is built with only the dynamically-discovered tools. The large language model (LLM) picks the right one(s) for the request, and the result is synthesized back to the user. After the turn finishes, the inner agent and its clients are torn down. The next request gets a fresh search and a fresh tool set. Figure 2: End-to-end architecture. A single orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime queries AWS Agent Registry. Matched MCP servers are invoked through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, and matched A2A agents are invoked on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime The reference architecture used in the sample includes AWS Agent Registry , Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime , Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Cognito, AWS Lambda, and AWS Secrets Manager. Three demo scenarios exercise the discovery loop with different capability combinations. The first is an MCP-only call (order status). The second chains MCP + A2A (pricing and discounts). The third tests a pure semantic match against ambiguous user intent: return and refund, where those words don’t appear in the matched A2A agent’s name. The linked runtime-discovery sample deploys the dependencies, creates and populates the Registry, verifies discovery, deploys the orchestrator, and runs three demos. orchestrator_agent.py contains the per-request discovery loop. utils.py parses Registry descriptors and creates MCP and A2A clients. cleanup.py removes resources. A Registry record contains a searchable description plus a protocol-specific descriptor. The sample uses the Agent Registry control-plane client for Registry and record lifecycle operations and the Agent Registry data-plane client for runtime discovery. Creating a Registry with manual approval and IAM authorization. The recordType field is required when creating a record. In this sample, MCP servers use recordType="MCP" and A2A-backed agents use recordType="AGENT" . Protocol metadata is stored under mcpServer or a2aAgentCard in the descriptors object. An MCP descriptor contains server metadata and tool definitions. An A2A descriptor contains the agent card. The descriptors contain connection metadata but not the credentials that a consumer must present when invoking the capability. Building current public-SDK descriptor shapes for MCP and A2A records. Write descriptions in user-facing language that distinguishes the capability from neighboring records. Descriptor content supplies the protocol-specific server, tool, or agent-card data. Search quality should be evaluated with representative queries. This post does not assume that catalog growth automatically improves ranking. Creating a Registry record with the current control-plane shape. With autoApproval set to false, a new record must move from DRAFT to PENDING_APPROVAL and then APPROVED . The submit and status-update actions are IAM-authorized , allowing publisher and approver permissions to be separated. Only approved records are returned by the discoverable Registry data plane. The two-step approval transition. The data-plane client supports hybrid keyword and semantic search across discoverable records. The latest method name is search_discoverable_registry_records . Results expose normalized record fields and discoverable descriptors. They don’t expose the capability’s invocation credentials. Searching approved, discoverable records across protocols. In the sample scenario, a return-and-refund query retrieves the Customer Support Agent because its description captures that intent. Treat this as a demo result, not a general claim that ranking improves merely because the catalog is larger. The orchestrator is a Strands agent deployed to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime . It exposes discover_and_execute , which searches the Registry, parses each returned descriptor, creates the corresponding MCP or A2A client, and builds a request-scoped inner agent from only those discovered capabilities. Figure 3: The orchestrator’s per-request flow. The outer agent translates the user request into a Registry search. The inner agent is assembled from the search results and torn down at the end of the turn The core of discover_and_execute fits in a single code block: The orchestrator’s discover/instantiate/execute loop. The sample fans out several search queries to improve recall for its order-management domain, deduplicates records, and tears down MCP clients after the request. That fan-out is a sample-specific orchestration choice, not a Registry requirement.

title: Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS
abstract: When AI agents access databases, APIs, and sensitive business operations, establishing cryptographic identity through X.509 public key infrastructure (PKI) becomes a critical requirement. The core challenge is proving which agent made a request, preventing forgery between agents, and confirming that each agent acts only on behalf of an authorized user. Traditional approaches such as sharing API keys between components or passing OAuth tokens through agent chains fall short of the zero-trust requirements that enterprise deployments demand. Multi-agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations. However, MCP has no built-in authentication standard. It is transport-agnostic by design. This creates a critical gap: Without proper identity mechanisms, any component could impersonate an agent, replay intercepted credentials, or invoke tools without authorization. In this post, we show you how to address this gap using Keyfactor EJBCA combined with AWS services. EJBCA is a PKI platform that supports high-availability deployment, REST API automation, and Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) validation. The reference architecture uses four complementary security mechanisms. First, signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every agent call. Second, user-signed delegation assertions authorize agents without sharing credentials. Third, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any single token disclosure. Fourth, real-time OCSP revocation checking propagates credential changes immediately across all agents. The solution uses Amazon Bedrock for LLM inference through the AWS Strands Agents SDK . While this reference architecture uses a database as the protected resource, the same authentication pattern applies to any MCP-compatible tool server. Complete source code for all examples is available in the accompanying GitHub repository. Keyfactor provides a widely adopted machine identity management platform used by more than 1,500 enterprise customers worldwide, according to Keyfactor. These organizations span financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, and government. Keyfactor helps organizations establish and maintain cryptographic trust through certificate lifecycle management, PKI operations, and machine identity governance. EJBCA Enterprise is Keyfactor’s Certificate Authority (CA) and PKI platform, designed for high-availability deployment and REST API automation. Available as an enterprise product, EJBCA provides X.509 certificate issuance, OCSP validation, certificate revocation list (CRL) distribution, and full certificate lifecycle management through both a web console and REST API. EJBCA supports deployment on-premises, in containers, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). The partnership between AWS and Keyfactor brings together AWS managed services (Amazon Bedrock, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)) with PKI infrastructure that supports certificate lifecycle management, automated enrollment, and real-time revocation. This combination addresses a gap in the AI agent ecosystem. While AWS provides the compute, storage, and AI inference layers, Keyfactor provides the cryptographic identity layer that binds agents to verifiable, revocable, short-lived credentials. This joint reference architecture, developed collaboratively by the AWS and Keyfactor engineering teams, demonstrates how to integrate these technologies. You can adapt the patterns shown here to your own multi-agent deployments. The architecture implements three authentication layers, each addressing a different trust boundary in the agent communication chain. These three layers use the four security mechanisms introduced earlier: signed envelopes for proof-of-possession, delegation assertions for credential-free authorization, audience-scoped tokens for exposure limitation, and OCSP for real-time revocation. The mechanisms combine across layers as shown in the following table. Figure 1 shows the three authentication layers and how credentials flow between the user, agents, and the MCP tool server. The diagram illustrates the separation between user credentials (which stay in the login flow), agent credentials (scoped per agent), and the delegation chain that connects them. Figure 1: Three-layer PKI authentication architecture for AI agent systems on AWS Figure 2 illustrates the detailed traffic flow during a typical user session. It shows the sequence of authentication steps from login through certificate issuance, agent delegation, tool invocation, and session cleanup. Figure 2: Authentication traffic flow from user login through agent delegation, tool invocation, and session cleanup The following AWS services form the foundation of the reference architecture. The following steps walk through each component of the architecture, from initial user login through to session cleanup. Each step builds on the previous one, establishing a chain of trust that connects the human user to the final tool execution. The login flow establishes the user’s identity through three mechanisms and then delegates authority to the AI agents without sharing the user’s credentials. This separation is critical: Agents receive proof of authorization without ever holding the user’s private key or full-session OAuth token. First, the application authenticates the user against Keycloak using an OAuth 2.0 password grant, receiving a full-session access token and refresh token. Immediately after, the application performs an RFC 8693 token exchange to obtain a downscoped token. This token’s audience is restricted to the MCP server. Only this limited token is handed to agents. If it’s inadvertently exposed, it can’t access any other service in the organization. Second, the application generates an RSA 2048+ key pair locally and submits a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) to EJBCA through the pkcs10enroll REST API endpoint. EJBCA signs the CSR and returns the certificate. The application bundles the certificate and private key into a PKCS12 container and stores it in AWS Secrets Manager. The private key never leaves the application boundary. It is not sent to EJBCA, not shared with agents, and not stored on the filesystem. Three agent certificates are issued using the same CSR-based flow, one per agent role. Third, the user’s private key signs a delegation assertion. This is a JSON document listing the SHA-256 fingerprints of all three agent certificates, along with the user’s subject name, issuance time, and expiry. This delegation proves that the user authorized these specific agents to act on their behalf. Agents carry this delegation instead of the user’s certificate. When the orchestrator agent routes a request to a sub-agent (such as the MySQL agent or Email agent), it does not simply pass its certificate for identification. Instead, it signs the entire request payload, including the tool name, arguments, a timestamp, and a cryptographically random nonce, using its private key with RSA-PSS-SHA256 . The resulting signed envelope provides proof-of-possession. The receiving agent can verify that the caller actually holds the private key corresponding to the presented certificate. The receiving agent performs six validation checks on the envelope before processing the request: If the orchestrator needs to re-send the same prompt (for example, after a transient failure), it must create a new envelope with a fresh nonce. Old envelopes can’t be replayed, even by the legitimate sender. The MCP server (FastMCP) is the final trust boundary before any database operation runs. It performs four validation checks on every tool invocation, implementing defense-in-depth.

title: How Eon built multi-cloud investigation with an MCP Gateway on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: This is a guest post co-written with Roei Zavida from Eon. Independent software vendors (ISVs) building AI-powered products need to connect agents and humans to dozens of operational tools across clouds, each with different authentication models, network boundaries, and access policies. When those tools span AWS, GCP, and Azure simultaneously, the integration surface multiplies. This post describes how Eon used Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Eon used it to replace per-tool credentials and local Model Context Protocol (MCP) processes with a single authenticated gateway. The result gives developers and autonomous agents unified access to investigation tooling across three clouds. New engineers now reach all their investigation tools in about two minutes instead of the two days it previously took to configure credentials and local MCP servers. Eon provides the Autonomous Data Foundation for the AI era. The platform discovers and classifies cloud resources across AWS, Azure, and GCP. It provides continuous deduplicated backup that reduces storage costs by up to 50 percent in Eon’s internal measurements. It also detects ransomware and rogue-agent damage and delivers live grounded context for AI agents. All of this runs from a single read-only AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, storing data in Apache Parquet and Apache Iceberg formats. Founded by former AWS engineers, Eon runs its software as a service (SaaS) infrastructure on AWS. Eon’s internal engineering team investigates production incidents across multiple clouds and dozens of operational systems. A crashed Kubernetes pod requires checking container logs, Grafana metrics, the deployment’s GitHub pull request (PR), and cloud-provider health status within the same session. Eon needed to address several key requirements: Growing engineering headcount combined with a fast-expanding set of AI tools and MCPs made maintaining credentials and local MCP servers increasingly costly. This pushed Eon toward a centralized solution. Before building on AgentCore, Eon evaluated alternatives: Every harness had its own proxy configuration with all the targets. A single reverse proxy aggregating all tools, with a custom authentication layer. This handled credential consolidation but only supported remote MCP and required building and maintaining tool protocol translation, session management, and authorization logic from scratch. The implementation and maintenance burden was significant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is a managed gateway with built-in identity federation, Cedar-based authorization policies, and Runtime hosting that converts local MCP servers to remote HTTP endpoints. This addressed all requirements without custom infrastructure. Eon chose Option 2 because it provided identity separation, cross-account connectivity, and policy enforcement as managed capabilities rather than code they would need to build and maintain. These were the only two options on the table. Eon deployed the full Amazon Bedrock AgentCore stack: AgentCore Gateway, Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, AgentCore Runtime, and AgentCore Identity, all capabilities of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The following diagram shows how client requests flow through the authentication layer to a single gateway. The gateway routes authorized tool calls to targets hosted on AgentCore Runtimes across multiple AWS accounts. Figure 1: Eon’s centralized gateway architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore The architecture has five layers: Developers using Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenAI Codex connect to a single MCP URL. An autonomous SRE agent running Claude on Amazon Bedrock connects to the same gateway with a different identity. Corporate single sign-on (SSO) federates through Amazon Cognito, which mints the JSON Web Token (JWT) and hands it to the gateway. Amazon API Gateway sits in front as the OAuth entry point for humans, proxying the MCP session. Agents authenticate with Cognito client_credentials grants directly against the gateway. A single AgentCore MCP Gateway serves as the company-wide front door. Cedar policies in ENFORCE mode control which principals can invoke which tools. Read operations are available to selected groups, not every authenticated user. Write operations are limited to low-impact collaboration actions, such as commenting on a PR or ticket, and production tools are read-only. Cedar policies map each principal to permitted tools. Write operations are limited to low-impact collaboration actions, such as commenting on a PR or ticket, and production tools are read-only. The gateway evaluates every tools/call request against Cedar before forwarding to the target. Dozens of target MCP servers exposing hundreds of tools on the one gateway, served by AgentCore Runtimes distributed across multiple AWS accounts. Each Runtime converts local stdio-based MCP servers into Streamable HTTP endpoints accessible through the gateway. A developer opens their integrated development environment (IDE), configures one MCP URL, authenticates through corporate SSO, and the gateway aggregates hundreds of tools into a single tools/list response. No local setup and no per-tool tokens. The core security decision was enforcing read and write boundaries through Cedar policy at the gateway level. Single gateway, policy-enforced separation: The gateway accepts both JWT tokens (humans through corporate SSO and Cognito) and client_credentials tokens (agents). Cedar policies determine what each principal can do. Humans in approved groups get read access. Write operations require explicit Cedar permits granted only to specific agent identities. Cedar reinforces per-tool granularity: Cedar policies are managed as code through GitHub PRs with review comments, giving the team version control and audit trail on every permission change. Within the gateway, Cedar policies scope tool access by SSO group, and groups map to job role. Engineers have access to development and testing environments by default. Production access follows Eon’s security and compliance controls: it is read-only, granted just-in-time through an approval process, and audited. A new team member’s group is scoped the same way, by role rather than by which service they happen to own. Because every agent action is checked against Cedar in ENFORCE mode and scoped to a least-privilege tool set, the autonomous agent operates within safe, bounded limits. It can only invoke the specific tools its identity is explicitly permitted to call. “Before, our internal agent couldn’t reach the same investigation tools developers used. After, it uses the same Gateway with its own identity and a tighter tool set.” — Roei Zavida, Senior DevOps Engineer, Eon Eon runs Runtimes across multiple AWS accounts, organized by environment or service boundary. AgentCore Gateway reaches each Runtime through IAM cross-account role assumption. The Runtime in Account B trusts the AgentCore Gateway execution role in Account A through a standard IAM trust policy. Depending on each tool’s authentication and hosting model, Eon uses two primary attachment patterns. The following table summarizes when to use each pattern and gives an example. Most targets use Runtime + IAM. Eon only wraps a remote MCP to shrink its catalog or slot in a credential the gateway cannot otherwise supply. The following flow traces a developer investigating a production incident: Deploying to 100+ developers and approximately 10,000 sessions surfaced production challenges: Every tool schema that the gateway pre-indexes contributes to Cedar policy size. With dozens of targets exposing extensive tool manifests, Eon’s policy grew toward the size quota. The fix: DYNAMIC listing mode for high-tool-count targets.

title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Agentic AI applications need governed access to live enterprise data. That data can live in operational systems, analytical warehouses, SaaS applications, other clouds, or on premises. In the previous post in this series , we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift. A Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore queried that layer. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post uses the same customer 360 pattern, but swaps in a different semantic layer implementation and extends the source mix. Two things change here. First, the semantic layer is the Denodo Platform: an AI data layer that provides active context and live, zero-copy access to distributed enterprise data. The agent talks to it in VQL , Denodo’s SQL dialect. Second, the source mix includes an on-premises PostgreSQL database alongside Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift, so the federation problem is no longer bounded by an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). The rest of the pattern carries over. A foundation model on Amazon Bedrock plans and writes queries. The Denodo MCP Server exposes governed views to the agent through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the agent, terminates inbound authentication, and manages the outbound credential the agent presents to Denodo. Everything the model reasons over lives inside the semantic layer rather than the prompt: the joins, the metric definitions, and the row and column filters that apply to the caller. By the end of this post, you will know: We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the previous post: what it is, what it’s for, and why the model plans query without owning the joins. If any of that is new, the previous post covers the ground. We stay with the same customer 360 pattern from the previous post. The Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit used in the previous article models an ecommerce retailer with two motivating use cases: understanding churn and identifying customers for auto-enrollment in a rewards program. The schema doesn’t change in this post. What changes is where one table lives: rewards_account sits on an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster rather than in Amazon Aurora with the rest of the customer profile data. That placement isn’t a special case. Enterprise data sources might be outside AWS: on premises, in a SaaS tool like a CRM, or in another cloud. The semantic layer must reach whichever applies. We use on-premises PostgreSQL for the walkthrough that represents data from a third-party application. The Extending to other sources section covers what changes when the source is a SaaS tool, a CRM, or a mainframe. It also covers the other hundreds of data sources that Denodo supports by default . The shared identifier is cid , a plain integer that appears as the primary key in the Aurora customer table. It appears as a non-foreign-key column in the Amazon Redshift order table and the on-premises rewards_account . Within Aurora itself, the customer.location column is an integer foreign key to address.id , which is how the profile joins to the address record. There is no foreign key that spans two engines, and no ETL job to build one. Answers that join customers to their purchases and their rewards enrollment must reconcile cid at query time. A representative question this setup answers: “Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?” This is the auto-enrollment scenario from the Stardog kit, and it needs profile data from Aurora, lifetime spend from Amazon Redshift, and enrollment status from the on-premises cluster to answer. Denodo plans the federated query at execution time, deciding what to push into Aurora, what to push into Amazon Redshift, what to fetch from the on-premises cluster, and how to combine the results. No data moves between sources, and the semantic layer stays declared once for every consumer to reuse. Denodo implements the semantic layer as a data virtualization platform. Denodo Virtual DataPort (VDP) is the query engine at the core: it’s where the semantic-layer objects live, where VQL executes, and where access policies evaluate. Design Studio is the browser-based authoring surface for VDP. Every object modeled in this post is defined there. Three object types come up repeatedly. VQL is Denodo’s SQL dialect. It’s ANSI-aligned SQL plus a set of Denodo-specific constructs, notably DDL constructs to represent data sources and syntax for semantic metric views. In an agentic scenario, the specific syntax of VQL is provided by a skill that will be used by the LLM when using Denodo tools to facilitate correct use of Denodo’s syntax. A Global Security Policy (GSP) is a runtime access-control rule that applies to views or columns carrying a specific tag. GSPs are how row filters and column masks get enforced at query time, evaluated per caller. For a fuller reference, see the Denodo Platform documentation . The runtime has two flows. Inbound: A client sends the user’s request to the agent through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP), then routes the request to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent process. The agent invokes a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 in this walkthrough) to interpret the prompt and plan the query. Outbound: AgentCore Gateway also acts as the outbound proxy for the agent’s tool calls. The Denodo MCP Server is registered as an MCP target on Gateway, so tool calls the agent makes for enterprise data route through Gateway to the MCP Server. Before the request reaches Denodo, AgentCore Identity performs an On-Behalf-Of token exchange , converting the human user’s inbound token into a scoped access token that represents the same user with Denodo as the audience. The Denodo MCP Server accepts the exchanged token as a bearer credential and forwards the VQL request to Denodo Virtual DataPort (VDP) over JDBC. VDP validates the token independently, resolves the caller to a Denodo role, applies access policies, and plans the federated query against Amazon Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. Only the VQL request travels down to VDP and the result set travels back up. No source data moves between engines. Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises cluster respond to native SQL rewritten by VDP’s federated optimizer. The following sections cover the identity propagation and policy enforcement in detail. Additional sections cover the MCP Server registration and agent deployment steps. Figure 1: Inbound authentication path and outbound query path between the caller, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore components, the Denodo MCP Server, Denodo Virtual DataPort, and the three data sources The semantic model in Denodo is not a single artifact. It’s a collection of base views, derived views, metric views, and tags in VDP that together present business-meaningful data to consumers. Building the semantic model in this post means creating each of those pieces. We build in three passes: base views over each source table, a derived view ( customer_360 ) that joins the base views on cid at the customer level, and a metric view ( lifetime_customer_value ) that defines a reusable spend aggregation queries can join in when they need it. In practice, this modeling is done visually in Denodo Design Studio. You drag Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises PostgreSQL source onto a canvas, draw joins between them, and rename or re-type fields (for example, mapping cust_ref to customer_id ) through a form rather than hand-written DDL. Attaching the security policies covered later in this post also happens inside the same UI.

title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Strategy Mosaic and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: This post is co-written with Zhili Cheng, Principal Product Manager, George Earle, Director, AI Engineering, and Kyler K, Sales Engineer of Strategy. In the first post in this series , we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift and ran a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore against that layer. The second post kept the same customer 360 (C360) pattern and swapped in Denodo’s data virtualization platform, extending the source mix to include an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. This post uses the same C360 pattern again, with Strategy Mosaic as the semantic layer. Stardog’s semantic layer is ontology-based: concepts and relationships modeled as RDF, with IRIs as the unit of federation and SPARQL as the query language. Denodo’s is data virtualization: base and derived views composed in VQL. Mosaic’s is dimensional: attributes, hierarchies, facts, and metrics composed through Strategy’s metric expression syntax, with linked models as the unit of federation. That model serves four native protocols from one definition: Model Context Protocol (MCP) for AI agents, JDBC/ODBC over Trino for SQL clients, XMLA for Power BI and Excel, and REST for custom applications. Behind those protocols is a long list of certified data sources . Supported systems include cloud warehouses such as Snowflake and Databricks.
