title: Called to serve: Tech, research, and positive impact
abstract: In the summer of 2010, postdoc Chris White worked with a multidisciplinary team at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, to determine if a new approach to data analysis could prevent violence and protect troops during the war in Afghanistan. At the conclusion of the program, the agency asked White to prove the value of his work—on the ground. In this episode, Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu talks with White, director of Catalyst Lab at Microsoft Research, about his unexpected break from academic research to help lead advanced tech operations in Afghanistan and his later decision to again work on tech with immediate, real-world implications: dark-web search tools used to help combat human trafficking. Liu and White explore the influences that led to these experiences plus the important role of problem selection in innovation and remaining hopeful after seeing the darkest parts of humanity. CHRIS WHITE: I have seen a lot of really bad humanity. You know, I’ve seen terrorism and trafficking and sophisticated organized crime, you know, designed to take things from people. Designed to hurt people. And I just know that I can do something about it, you know, and that I have and that we can. And so I think that that light, you know, the light of making a difference, you know, allows me to hold and handle, you know, the dark parts. STANDARD INTRODUCTION: This is the Microsoft Research Podcast , where Microsoft researchers—driving advancement through fundamental science and technology research—explore the who, how, and what’s next in computing and AI. WEISHUNG LIU: Hi, and welcome. I’m Weishung Liu, a principal technical program manager here at Microsoft Research, and today I’m talking to Dr. Christopher White, who leads Microsoft Research’s Catalyst Lab . Chris has one of those careers that sounds almost made up: a Harvard postdoc, on-the-ground advanced tech lead during the war in Afghanistan, a DARPA program manager, a dark web search pioneer, and a public-good technologist. And his work has been featured in Popular Science (opens in new tab) as well as recognized with honors, including the 2016 Presidential Award for Extraordinary Efforts to Combat Trafficking in Persons (opens in new tab) . But what I’m most interested in today is the person behind that résumé. How someone who has seen some of the worst as part of his work still comes to the office with a smile and a commitment to building tools that make the world better. WHITE: Thanks for having me, Wei. Nice to see you. LIU: Yeah, good to see you, too. And so let’s get started. So I’ve known you for, I think, maybe around five or maybe six years, and now I work with you in Catalyst Lab. I love your story, and when I tell people about you, I say that you lead the newly formed Cat Lab, or Catalyst Lab, in Microsoft Research, you were a senior executive at DARPA, and you are married to an incredibly accomplished woman and scholar. And I personally think that your life story would make a very watchable Hollywood film. So when you tell your own story, though, where do you start? WHITE: Well, you start from where you are. And where I am today is leading research at Microsoft during a period of great fear and hope about changing technology and society. LIU: But, like, that’s now. There’s clearly lots of time from now into before, you know, the before times. So, like, tell me a little bit about the before times. Like, where were you at—I think you grew up in Oklahoma maybe. Tell me about that. Tell me about Chris White, the child. WHITE: Well, I was nerdy. I was a nerdy Eagle Scout. [LAUGHTER] I liked to build my own computers and have local area network [LAN] parties with my friends. But I also really liked being outside. I liked being in nature and camping and rock climbing. Those were all important to me. LIU: OK, you mentioned LAN parties. Tell me about … what did we play with our friends? WHITE: Well, you know, we played everything. I preferred playing sports games, but I lost a lot of the other ones. LIU: [LAUGHS] Wait, so you played like LAN party sports games, like, in basements? Like, with your … were we all in the same … ? WHITE: Yeah. Attics. It was attics. Yeah, not basements. [LAUGHTER] Mm-hmm. Yeah. Everybody had to bring their own computer or bring their own Ethernet cable. And the more that you had your own machine that was higher powered, the better you were going to play. LIU: So did you have the best machine? WHITE: I had the best machine. I built the best machine. Until someone built a better machine. But it was the best for a while. And I had a budget for it. And my family didn’t understand that the budget also included two giant speakers, like the size of a computer tower, like subwoofer speakers. They didn’t know that was part of the computer building process. But it turns out that excellent audio-visual is a critical part of a well-functioning machine. LIU: I love it. But, OK, we’re going to focus a little bit … continue focusing on childhood. So you mentioned nerdy kid, which means—I’m going to generalize here—debate team or math competition team or chess team? WHITE: Oh, it was the debate team. Yeah. Debate was a really wonderful activity. It taught me how to understand many sides of an issue and taught me how to think about evidence and research in that way. LIU: So, Chris, take me back again. Like, we’re talking a little bit about Oklahoma, and, you know, at some point, you chose researcher. Like, I—for example—when I was a kid, I was convinced I would be an architect. I am not an architect as you can see. But did you always think you were going to be a researcher? Was there an epiphany there? Like … or was it always kind of like a slow hunch that you were going to pursue research as a career? WHITE: Yeah, I kind of always felt like it. You know, as I was applying for school, those were the kinds of jobs I was interested in. You know, the kinds of things that you do, you know, once you finish degrees that have research in them. Those were the people, when I visited their work, I was inspired by. The people that were discovering, you know, that were inventing, that were innovating, that were … they’re pushing the boundaries that were kind of in that unknown, you know, space and making sense of it. And so I’ve always had that curiosity, you know, and that approach to discovery. And so as I increased my education, it just changed the nature of what research meant and the ways in which I imagined that process evolving. LIU: Was a doctorate always on the cards then? Or did that come, like, as you were in college and then gradually learned and thought, you know, I could keep going? WHITE: Yeah, you know, I didn’t know about doctorates really when I went to college. I wasn’t as familiar with higher education. And so I knew that I wanted, you know, advanced degrees. And I knew that I wanted more than was being taught in the undergraduate level. But I didn’t know, you know, for example, that when you apply to PhD programs, that often you get paid to go. You know, you get admitted and you get a stipend. You know, I was familiar with law and medicine and that you take out loans and you have to do it this way. And so for me, it was a surprise to know that I could apply to PhD programs directly from college. And from then, I just really was excited, you know, that I could explore different universities and different areas of focus and build on, you know, strong technical foundations of math and science and physics. And it was really amazing mentors that helped me and opened doors and inspired me. You know, mentors at Oklahoma State University, Johns Hopkins, and Harvard, really people that took their time and helped me. I’m really grateful for my teachers. LIU: So let’s talk about your first mentor of your life, and I’m going to assume … Dad ? WHITE: Yeah, Dad’s a big influence. LIU: OK, Dad’s a big influence.

title: Strengthening AI safety evaluation through independent third-party review
abstract: As frontier AI models grow in capability, so does the importance of ensuring that safety evaluations are rigorous and comprehensive. At Amazon, we invest heavily in internal safety testing for our models, spanning categories like harmful-content generation, cybersecurity risks, privacy protection, and copyright compliance. A core principle of robust quality assurance is that even rigorous internal processes are strengthened by external scrutiny. That's why we partnered with AVERI (AI Verification and Evaluation Research Institute), an independent nonprofit dedicated to third-party evaluation of AI systems, to conduct an independent review of our internal safety evaluation datasets. AVERI’s mandate wasn’t just to test model outputs but to examine the quality and rigor of our tests themselves — asking whether our evaluations stress-test safety boundaries. How the collaboration worked We provided AVERI with a random sample of prompts drawn from our internal safety-evaluation suite. AVERI's team — led by executive director Miles Brundage and including researchers Sean McGregor, A. Feder Cooper, and George Balston — examined the evaluation prompts for diversity, difficulty calibration, and methodological soundness. AVERI assessed the sample independently without input from our evaluation team, ensuring their findings reflected a genuine external perspective. What the review confirmed AVERI’s review validated several strengths of our evaluation process: Comprehensive topical coverage — aligned with publicly documented safety categories including self-harm, cybersecurity, and other risk areas; Diversity of testing approaches — variation in writing style (professional vs. informal), single-turn and multiturn conversations, and original content; Low contamination risk — content that appeared to be original rather than sourced from publicly available datasets, reducing risk of evaluation leakage through pretraining. Opportunities for improvement With any fresh review comes the opportunity to identify areas that internal teams — deeply familiar with their own work — may overlook. AVERI's external perspective surfaced several opportunities to further strengthen an already comprehensive suite: Expanding linguistic and stylistic diversity — While our evaluations include multilingual prompts, AVERI recommended extending multilingual coverage more evenly across risk categories and further varying prompt structures to broaden the range of scenarios tested; Calibrating attack sophistication — AVERI recommended adding more multistep, adversarial prompts to our existing set, so evaluations probe deeper model reasoning and better reflect sophisticated real-world misuse attempts; Maintaining evaluation freshness — AVERI identified a small number of prompts with time-limited references and a few edge cases where grading criteria could be made clearer; Ensuring evaluation signal quality — In some cases, models may refuse based on superficial cues in a prompt, so passing those tests doesn’t necessarily indicate reliable safety behavior in new situations. How we incorporated the feedback Concrete improvements made: Test set refresh: Updated evaluation datasets to address specific issues identified, removing redundant prompts and adding more-challenging adversarial scenarios Difficulty calibration framework: Introduced tiered difficulty levels to ensure that evaluations include prompts that genuinely push model safety limits, not just straightforward cases Quarterly review cadence: Established a regular evaluation maintenance process to catch staleness, reduce repetition, and incorporate emerging attack patterns Broader language coverage: Expanded multilingual prompts across all risk categories rather than concentrating them in specific areas A model for the field This collaboration represents what we believe is an emerging best practice: engaging independent third parties to evaluate not just model outputs, but the quality of the evaluation process itself. As the AI safety field matures, we expect this kind of meta-evaluation to become an important complement to traditional red-teaming and benchmarking. The benefits are mutual: Amazon gains an independent check on our evaluation quality, while AVERI gains practical experience with the real-world challenges of assessing internal evaluation processes — insights that can inform best practices for the field as a whole. We're grateful to AVERI for their thorough and constructive review, and we plan to continue engaging independent evaluators as our models evolve. Transparency about our safety processes — including where we can improve — is fundamental to building justified confidence in AI safety.

title: MemCurrent: Designing Persistent Memory for Production Agents
abstract: AI tools have made it easy to vibe code agents. Building and maintaining an enterprise agent in production, however, remains significantly more challenging. In particular, developers are often forced to make a trade-off between quality (getting good answers, especially on long-tail tasks) and efficiency (keeping cost and latency in check at scale). Oftentimes, techniques bring gains in one dimension at the cost of another. Memory is a promising way to improve both at the same time. It can help agents carry useful context across tasks, such as user preferences, prior corrections, metric definitions, and successful workflows. In principle, this can improve accuracy, reduce repeated errors, and avoid unnecessary rediscovery. But more history is not necessarily better memory. Supplying every past interaction is costly and can introduce stale, conflicting, or irrelevant context. The central challenge is deciding what to retain, how to maintain it, and how to measure usefulness. In this post, we introduce MemCurrent , a persistent memory architecture for production agents, which now powers the new Agent Bricks Memory and Genie . Agents read and write memory as they work, and an offline “dreaming” pipeline consolidates memory to keep it consistent and fresh. On our internal benchmark, built from realistic enterprise tasks, MemCurrent triples the agent's pass rate over having no memory, while using 31% fewer tokens and running 26% faster. The rest of this post covers how we designed and evaluated it, and what we learned along the way. Figure 1. Pass rate vs. tokens per task on our Internal Memory Benchmark. MemCurrent is on the Pareto frontier, outperforming Mem0, PropMem, and OpenClaw memory on both dimensions. There are three ways to wire memory into an agent. As a plugin (like our earlier work on MemAlign and Memory Scaling ), memory is read and written automatically at fixed points in a session. As tools , the agent decides what and when to read and write. As an offline pipeline , memory is updated in the background on a schedule or trigger, and used in later sessions. Each comes with trade-offs: Table 1. Three access patterns of memory: plugin, tool, or offline pipeline. MemCurrent uses all three, each where it fits best. Figure 2. Overview of MemCurrent. MemCurrent has two types of memory: episodic memory , which stores raw session traces; and derived memory , which has the distilled learnings from these traces, stored as files in a structured knowledge base. An auto-generated memory.md index sits at the top, describing the file structure and what each file contains. Both episodic and derived memory live in a production-grade database that can scale to many users while delivering low-latency responses. Episodic memory is append-only, where a plugin logs each step as the session runs. Derived memory is a mutable table simulating a hierarchical file system, where writing happens in two ways. Agent tools ( add_memory, update_memory, delete_memory ) handle explicit requests like “Never write scripts in the /tmp dir”. An offline dreaming pipeline captures the rest, distilling implicit learnings from each new session into the relevant files. It also cleans up the whole store, splitting oversized files, merging duplicates, and resolving conflicts. Reading works in layers. At session start, a plugin injects the memory index, so the agent knows what it knows before it begins. During the session, the agent has two tools that work across both memory types: search_memory returns the top matches for a query (a step in a past trace, or a line in a memory file), and fetch_memory returns the full entry by identifier (session ID or file path). We start with three popular open-source benchmarks: LoCoMo , LongMemEval , and ConvoMem . All three test whether an agent can recall facts stated earlier in open-ended synthetic conversations. In addition, we built an Internal Memory Benchmark from real Genie conversations, where users ask all kinds of questions about their data. As in Figure 3, we started from 12K+ sessions, mined 3K candidates containing memory-worthy signals, and drafted a follow-up question with scoring rubrics. The other sessions from the same user serve as fillers for the test case. An adversarial judge then checked each test case against 7 criteria, such as whether the knowledge is actually present, specific to the user, required to answer, natural, and verifiable. After a final manual review, the benchmark has a total of 114 test cases, with 29 users and 2,233 history sessions. Figure 3. How we built our Internal Memory Benchmark. Figure 4. An example test case from our Internal Memory Benchmark. In a past session, the user corrects the agent's choice of table and tells it to exclude background requests. Later, the agent faces a different but related question, and has to find that session among 100+ others and apply what it learned. The output is scored by an LLM judge based on a list of rubrics (some memory-dependent, some task-intrinsic). Our benchmark differs from existing ones in three ways: Enterprise domain. Existing benchmarks are open-ended chats about the lives of simulated personas. Ours is from real work in a data workspace, involving rich enterprise knowledge like table semantics, metric definitions, and workflows. Memory feeds actions, not answers. Finding the right string in past conversations is not enough; agents must apply retrieved knowledge to complete multi-step tasks. Diversity. Test cases span 5 memory types (profile, preferences, domain knowledge, projects, workflows) crossed with 11 scenarios (direct instruction, changing or outdated facts, multi-session aggregation, memory-independent questions, and more). We compare MemCurrent with three open-source memory backends, Mem0 , PropMem , OpenClaw memory , using the same underlying LLM. Open-Source Benchmarks. We pair each memory backend with a simple question-answering agent, built with two agent harnesses (LangGraph and OpenAI Agents SDK). We also run two baselines: a floor with no memory , and a ceiling with full context , where every past session goes into the agent's context. Across all three benchmarks, MemCurrent scores highest among all memory backends and stays on the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier . On average, MemCurrent (88.1%) performs on par with full context (87.8%) at ~12x fewer input tokens per question (8.4K vs 103K). On the two benchmarks with the longest histories, it even beats full context, where dumping everything into the prompt ends up confusing the agent. Figure 5. Cost–accuracy 1 trade-off of memory backends on (a) LoCoMo (19–32 sessions/sample), (b) LongMemEval (s split) (38–62 sessions/sample), and (c) ConvoMem (stratified subset of 500 samples, 100 sessions/sample). We use GPT 5.6 luna as the agent and memory model. All memory backends are run as a plugin, which automatically searches for related memories to the question and injects them into the agent context at session start. 2 Accuracy is the mean over the LangGraph and OpenAI Agents SDK harnesses and 3 repeats. Cost is mean input tokens per question (log scale). Internal Memory Benchmark. On our benchmark, the gap widens. Here, each memory backend runs inside our internal Genie, the same agent the benchmark sessions came from. The histories are too long to fit in context, so our ceiling is gold injection: injecting only the gold memories into the agent's context. Among all memory backends, MemCurrent has the highest pass rate (68.4%) and the lowest latency (252s) and token usage (418K), closing over 80% of the gap between no memory (22.3%) and gold injection (78.6%). Notably, while Mem0 was also on frontier on earlier benchmarks, it trails at 43.9% here with higher latency and cost. Compared to no memory, MemCurrent triples the agent's pass rate (22.3% → 68.4%) while making it 1.35x faster and 1.44x cheaper . Figure 6.

title: Introducing Agent Memory on Databricks
abstract: Today we're introducing agent memory on Agent Bricks, Databricks' agent developer platform. Agent memory improves agent quality while decreasing costs and latency by storing critical facts, preferences, and workflows that an agent should remember. It's available in Beta today, runs on Lakebase for high reliability and low latency, and is built on Databricks' latest memory research. Without memory, agents risk rediscovering key facts, forgetting user preferences, and repeat mistakes it was already corrected on. In response, many developers are rolling their own memory solutions, but run into numerous design questions - for example, where should memories be stored? How should memories get synthesized? And once generated, how should they be retrieved? To address this, Databricks Agent Memory is built on the MemCurrent architecture, pioneered by Databricks Research . MemCurrent combines three access patterns: plugins to log and load context automatically, tools the agent calls on demand, and an offline dreaming pipeline that consolidates memory in the background. All of this is served with extremely low latency using Lakebase. In our internal benchmarks, implementing this memory architecture tripled agent pass rate on real enterprise tasks while using 31% fewer tokens. Agent Memory joins the rest of Agent Bricks, including agent hosting, Databricks Sandbox, Unity Gateway, pre-built MCP servers, and tracing and evaluation, providing developers all the infrastructure capabilities needed to build production agents. Two problems show up as soon as an agent moves from a demo to daily use. Agent developers, and the platform teams that run their agents, have two common workarounds. Each one trades one problem for another: What teams need is memory that makes agents cheaper and more personal at the same time, without standing up another system to get it. Figure 1. Agent Memory on Agent Bricks. The agent appends each turn to managed sessions, recalls and saves memories directly, and a memory pipeline distills sessions into long-term memory in the background. Everything runs on Lakebase, Databricks' serverless Postgres, provisioned in your workspace and operated by Databricks. This ensures that storing and retrieving memories is lightning fast, and that your stores can scale along with your agent traffic. Agent Memory is a production implementation of MemCurrent, the memory system described in MemCurrent: Designing Memory for Enterprise Agents . Our researchers’ central finding is that memory works best in two layers: a raw record of what happened, and a distilled record of what's worth remembering, kept current by a background process rather than written ad hoc by the agent mid-task. Built that way, memory improved quality and efficiency at the same time. Agents passed about three times as many tasks as agents without memory, finished faster, and used fewer tokens. The same infrastructure already powers memory in Genie, Databricks' natural-language experience for business users. Figure 2. Agents with and without memory on Databricks' internal memory benchmark of enterprise data tasks. Source: MemCurrent research. None of this requires new infrastructure on your side. The Agent Bricks CLI can help you deploy an agent with memory and sessions in minutes. From then on, your agent's next conversation with each user starts with what it learned from the previous ones. For more info, see the quickstart to create a new agent with memory, or our tutorial for adding memory to an existing agent. Agent Memory is one part of Agent Bricks, Databricks' agent developer platform for building, running, and improving custom agents at scale, with any model, framework, or harness. Explore Agent Bricks to see the rest of the platform. Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: How Hamlet uses Databricks Lakebase Postgres to test changes against production data
abstract: Hamlet, an AI-powered platform that makes local government decision-making accessible and searchable, uses Databricks Lakebase Postgres to give every pull request its own branch of production data. Engineers and AI coding agents test changes against real data without touching production, and a person still approves every merge. I spoke with CEO Sunil Rajaraman, Lead Developer Erich Douglass and Senior AI Engineer Jeff Hui about how they work. Hamlet is an AI-powered technology platform that makes local government decision-making accessible and searchable. By indexing and transcribing thousands of city council, planning commission, and zoning board meetings across the U.S., Hamlet allows real estate developers, journalists, researchers, and citizens to instantly search meeting transcripts, track local policy developments, and set up real-time alerts for specific topics, addresses, or businesses. Sara Steffen: Hamlet indexes meetings from more than 7,200 governing bodies across every state. What does that data landscape look like, and why is it so hard to make sense of? Sunil Rajaraman: There are 19,000 city governments, 3,000 county governments and roughly 80,000 special districts in the United States. Pick any two of their websites and they won’t look alike. That’s the original sin of local government. A handful of CMS providers decided every site should be different, and the result is an internet of government that’s completely balkanized. Hamlet pulls all of it together and standardizes it. Erich Douglass: You can’t just integrate with one provider. Seven or eight of them cover about 75% of the market. After that it’s a massive long tail of custom setups. Sometimes a clerk uploads a PDF of the agenda. Sometimes they scan a paper copy and upload that. You get some really weird artifacts. Sara: Hamlet describes itself as a civic intelligence platform. How is that different from a transcription tool, and why does the distinction matter? Sunil: A lot of govtech companies are an arbitrage of municipal data. They write brittle scrapers for 1998-era websites and put a modern coat of paint on top. Scraping and storing the data doesn’t add much on its own. You have to tell a story, and it has to be based on fact. That means knowing who’s speaking and how they feel about an issue. If you’re a developer, you want to know whether a council member will approve your housing project, why or why not, and what history the city has that might make it hesitate. Look at permitting. A lot of venture money has gone into permitting data, and permitting timelines have still gotten worse over the past decade. Many companies have built monuments to the symptoms. We want to get to the underlying problem, which is understanding people. The question we’re trying to answer is how cities fundamentally work. Sara Steffen: What makes local government data so difficult to work with? Sunil Rajaraman: Pick any two of their websites and they won’t look alike. Hamlet pulls it all together and standardizes it. Erich Douglass: You can’t just integrate with one provider. Seven or eight of them cover about 75% of the market. After that it’s a massive long tail of custom setups. Sometimes a clerk uploads a PDF of the agenda. Sometimes they scan a paper copy and upload that. You get some really weird artifacts. Sara: What do customers need from that data? Sunil: Our customers are private companies like real estate developers, data center developers and retailers. Nearly all of them are trying to get a project approved faster or find a new opportunity. Without Hamlet, someone sits through hours of meetings, waits for their project to come up and watches the officials’ body language. We identify who spoke, take you to the timestamp and show you the receipts. Erich: They also want precedent. Has a project like theirs been approved or rejected before? Why? What changes did the council ask for? If we can show what’s really going on, that’s a lot of value. Sara: How do you help customers trust the insights they find? Jeff Hui: We use it in almost every part of the process. Early on, Hamlet did this work by hand, and that doesn’t scale to thousands of places. For a lot of these governments, the video is the primary source of truth. Getting it into a structured form we can use is the most important part. The average meeting runs about three and a half hours. Nobody wants to watch all of it. AI points people to the parts worth their time, and the video is always there to back it up. We can show exactly what was said, which a lot of AI systems struggle to do. Sara: How do you identify speakers accurately across thousands of meetings? Jeff: Context makes the biggest difference. For speaker identification, we know which council or committee is meeting and who was on it at the time. That helps with names, which are hard to get right even for a person listening to a recording. You can’t hand a model a video and hope for the best. You have to collect everything around it that helps it make the right call. It’s a forever challenge. Sara: How do you check the AI’s interpretation of what officials say? Sunil: Accurate transcription comes first. For sentiment, we use multiple AI models to confirm a comment is about a given topic, say data centers. Then they look at the surrounding context to decide whether it’s for or against. You also have to define what pro and anti mean before you ask. Take policing. What does being for it mean? We put a lot of care into those questions. Several models now review every sentiment figure before we publish it, and we require high confidence. Lakebase is the managed Postgres database Hamlet uses to give each pull request its own branch of production data. Engineers can test changes against the data that caused a bug without touching production, while AI coding agents run the pipelines and check their work before a person approves the merge. The team says its previous test-data setup could take several hours per engineer each week. Sara: Why did you choose Lakebase, and what changed for your team? Erich: We had a pretty standard setup on AWS RDS, with one production instance and one staging instance. A lot of our work is tuning data pipelines against very specific data. For every pull request, we’d spend 15 to 30 minutes getting staging into the right state before we could run validations. We’re a small team, and velocity matters to us more than almost anything. Data branching was the feature that sold us. Every pull request now gets its own branch of production data, connected to its preview environment. When the preview deploys, it’s ready. We can test against production data and even write to it without touching production. Autoscaling helps too. On RDS, a bigger instance meant a migration that could take a couple of hours. Now we move a slider and get twice as big an instance. Jeff: The 15 to 30 minutes was the best case, when you happened to copy exactly the right data. Each engineer could spend several hours a week keeping test data current, including cloning pieces of production locally to chase down issues. Now when we hit a bug, we have the exact data that caused it, and we can check the fix against that same data. Sara: How does Lakebase change the way your AI coding agents work? Jeff: Branches make our workflow a much better fit for AI coding agents. Each pull request is isolated from production. We give an agent like Claude or Codex access to its branch and let it run its own checks. It runs the data pipelines to completion and looks at whether the change does what it should. Every pull request gets that first pass from an agent. By the time a person looks at it, we’re already fairly confident it works. A human still approves the merge. More and more of the rest is automated, and Lakebase is a big part of what makes that possible. Sara: What are you exploring next with Lakebase?

title: How HP Is Building an AI-Ready CDP with Databricks CustomerLake
abstract: At Data + AI Summit 2026, Luis Alonso , Global Head of Data Strategy & Engineering for MarTech & AI Enablement at HP, shared how the company is building an AI-ready go-to-market data foundation on Databricks. HP has spent extensive time and effort unifying customer data and third-party signals in their Marketing Lakehouse, and now Genie and CustomerLake make that trusted context available to marketers making daily decisions about audiences, channels, and customer journeys. HP’s early work highlights three ways this approach can reduce costs, expand available customer context, and accelerate activation: For HP, a CDP isn't one product or a narrow set of activation features. It's a collection of capabilities built around the needs of the business: As HP consolidated more governed data and business logic on Databricks, maintaining a separate CDP increasingly meant duplicating pipelines, data and operational overhead. Composable architectures reduced some data movement, but the activation layer still lacked the business definitions, context, and governance already available in the data platform. That context is essential for self-service analytics and AI agents. Without it, an agent may be able to access data but still lack the definitions, relationships, metrics and governance needed to use it correctly. HP's broader data transformation consolidated hundreds of data lakes and repositories into a small number of Databricks lakehouses. The company uses central standards with federated execution, allowing domain experts to retain ownership and stewardship while sharing governed data products across the business. This gave marketing governed access to previously fragmented sources, including media performance, market-share, technographic and intent data, along with propensity models. The change has materially changed how HP teams work together. Alonso described a 2024 request to share data with a sales partner that required three months, roughly 15 email exchanges and three escalations, without a reliable outcome. Today, a comparable request can result in a governed Delta Sharing asset within 48 hours. That improvement gives marketing faster access to the data it needs for planning, targeting, reporting and measurement, while preserving domain ownership and governance. Creating a strong technical foundation doesn't automatically make data usable for marketers. The next step is enabling executives, marketing users, media teams and analysts to use that foundation without relying on engineering for every question or task. HP is using AI/BI Genie and agent-based capabilities to help bridge that gap across three layers of work: Business context is a core part of that strategy. HP is developing semantic layers that help Genie understand what the company's data means, including domains, metric views, instructions and reusable skills. For example, HP created a media metric view covering 26 dimensions and 10 measures. This centralizes definitions for media-spend and performance KPIs so dashboards, business users and AI systems can work from the same source of truth. HP has also expanded its intent-data ingestion from 75 topics to approximately 20,000 topics. Genie Code helps the team plan how to cluster those signals at scale and use them for richer account profiles. HP is also rethinking where identity resolution should live. Historically, companies often sent customer data to an external identity provider and kept the resulting identity layer outside their core data environment. HP plans to bring identity signals back into its Databricks environment. That creates a governed foundation for measurement, audience activation and model improvement. Data can flow through the same identity service on its way to media platforms and on the return path, helping HP build a more complete view of performance and continuously improve its models. Alonso noted that reaching even 10% of HP's consumer customer base through this consent-preserving approach could create a substantial new opportunity for the commercial business. HP's early experience with CustomerLake illustrates the potential of bringing marketing capabilities directly to the governed data foundation. Based on the team's prior CDP implementations, Alonso expected a long setup process involving extensive meetings, documentation, data-model configuration, and privacy and security reviews. The initial experience was dramatically simpler. “We had our data models in place, we had attributes published, and we were ready to build audiences — work that might have previously required two or three months to complete.” Because CustomerLake is native to Databricks and Unity Catalog, HP's team could work directly with their schemas, tables, definitions, and governance, instead of recreating context in a separate platform. The architecture also supports a significant B2C-to-B2B opportunity. HP has hundreds of millions of consumer customers, but a much smaller known population of business contacts. CustomerLake makes it possible for HP to work across both their B2C and B2B data models and systems in one environment through a shared identity layer. HP can also incorporate data from other platforms using Lakehouse Federation. Across the go-to-market roadmap, HP is evaluating value in three areas: HP’s work with Genie and CustomerLake suggests potential to address all three areas together. Their journey offers four practical takeaways for other enterprises modernizing their marketing stack: HP’s journey shows that modernizing marketing activation and applying AI at scale both depend on bringing data, intelligence, and action together on the same foundation. With CustomerLake and Genie on its governed Marketing Lakehouse, HP is giving marketers and agents direct access to trusted context without recreating it across disconnected systems. The early results include becoming audience-ready in two hours instead of months, with the potential to reduce CDP TCO by up to 40%. Together, these gains lay the foundation for faster, more intelligent and more personalized customer engagement at scale. Watch the full Data + AI Summit session here.
