title: CustomerLake enters Beta: Leading enterprises going live with the Agentic CDP
abstract: Today, we’re excited to share a major CustomerLake milestone: Campaign Agents is advancing to Beta and Profile Agents is entering Private Preview. This marks the next stage of product maturity for the Agentic CDP embedded in Databricks, and expands participation to more customers. When we introduced CustomerLake at Data + AI Summit , we outlined a new operating model for marketing: embed your CDP into the governed data and AI platform where your most complete customer context already lives. Since then, brands like Getnet by Santander, HP, and AB InBev have been using CustomerLake to understand their audiences more deeply and give marketers greater freedom to deliver more tailored campaigns and better customer experiences. AI is raising the stakes for marketing speed and relevance. 74% of consumers use AI to discover, compare, or purchase products. As agents take on more of the buying journey at machine speed, marketers need agents of their own to recognize changing intent and respond in real time. Databricks is where enterprise data, AI models, and governance already come together, giving CustomerLake agents the trusted context to act. The customer stories below show CustomerLake’s three core principles in action: Embedded, Democratized, and Autonomous . Hyper-personalized campaigns are only possible with a complete and consistent view of the customer. Enterprises already invest in Databricks to define their data, maintain quality, and govern how it’s used. CustomerLake makes that work available to marketers, reducing the need to recreate customer context in another platform. For HP , using their Marketing Lakehouse foundation has accelerated audience turnaround while reducing martech cost of ownership. Read more about how HP is building an AI-ready CDP with Databricks CustomerLake . Getnet by Santander is connecting transactional, behavioral, and predictive intelligence so commercial, CRM, and marketing teams can work from a complete view of the customer. Customer intelligence is most valuable in the hands of the people closest to the customer. CustomerLake gives those teams the freedom to explore customer context and immediately act on what they learn. Zé Delivery, part of AB InBev , is enabling greater ownership of live campaigns for its CRM team without dependence on data engineering. CustomerLake makes enterprise data that was previously difficult to bring into marketing tools directly available for audience building and activation, through the engagement platforms marketing teams already use. A growing customer base shouldn’t mean more generic marketing. CustomerLake’s agentic approach helps marketers use richer customer context to make personalization more targeted as audiences grow, without multiplying the manual work behind each campaign. For Wine.com , that means turning a vast catalog and diverse customer tastes into opportunities for more relevant, precisely targeted campaigns. Philadelphia Union’s ambition is to turn a surge of interest from the FIFA World Cup into a lasting relationship with each individual fan. We’re putting CustomerLake to work in our own marketing, too. For Data + AI Summit, we used CustomerLake to personalize session recommendations for 30,000 in-person attendees. Campaign Agents evaluated each person’s engagement history to craft an email reflecting the recipient’s interests and behavior, helping attendees discover the sessions most relevant to them. The campaign delivered a 10 point conversion lift against a control group, a 10% click-through rate and a 60% open rate , outperforming every previous Summit email campaign. It shows how trusted customer context can inform both who to engage and what to recommend. Campaign Agents is now in Beta, opening participation to more customers who meet the technical requirements. As participation expands, delivery partner Stitch has seen how CustomerLake can accelerate the path to marketing self-service across its client base. The results above show meaningful progress: faster audience turnaround, greater marketer independence, and personalized recommendations at scale. These are the building blocks for CustomerLake’s broader vision of Infinity Campaigns : continuous, agent-driven engagement loops that analyze customer signals, determine relevant actions, and adapt as customer context changes. Each step gives marketers more room to shape the customer experience and less time coordinating the mechanics behind it. People set the strategy, goals, and guardrails; agents help scale execution. Profile Agents, entering Private Preview today, helps data teams unify scattered customer information from dozens of sources into trusted Customer 360 profiles directly in Databricks, giving marketers a consistent customer view for better segmentation and personalization. Its capabilities address three connected tasks: Profile Agents and Campaign Agents can be adopted independently. Teams can start with campaign workflows using their existing customer data or use Profile Agents to improve how they prepare and unify customer records. AI in marketing can only work safely and effectively at scale when agents have governed access to trusted customer data, models, and business context. CustomerLake brings these together in Databricks, giving agents the intelligence and guardrails to make relevant decisions that achieve business goals. Customers are already demonstrating what this new operating model for agentic marketing can deliver. Now, more organizations can put their Databricks investments to work for customer engagement. To get access to CustomerLake, contact your Databricks account team. Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: How to get the most out of running dbt on Databricks
abstract: Tens of thousands of organizations rely on dbt for data transformation. Where you run it shapes everything: how much it costs to run your dbt pipelines, how fast they ship, and how much operational work they carry. Running dbt on Databricks gives your dbt workloads an open platform and a unified pipeline . Over 3000 organizations run dbt on Databricks, and most teams could be getting a lot more out of it. This blog highlights the practices that make dbt pipelines cheaper, faster, and simpler to operate on Databricks. dbt bills climb from work you don't need to repeat. Full rebuilds recompute data that hasn't changed, keeping queries fast takes manual-tuning, and when the bill spikes there's no clear attribution back to the dbt models that caused it. Adopt the practices in this section and your pipelines will: Full table rebuilds are the largest avoidable cost in most dbt projects. When only a small fraction of the data changes between runs, recomputing the entire table wastes your compute and increases your bill. dbt's incremental strategies , all supported on dbt-databricks, let each model process only new data, and the right choice depends on how your data actually arrives. Rows are only ever inserted, never updated The same key can arrive more than once and needs upserting (slowly changing dimensions, dedupe, late-arriving updates) The model re-derives a narrow time window each run, such as the last few days of activity Your query returns whole partitions You want records replaced by key, without column-level update logic Time-series data with an event_time column and structured backfill needs Most projects default to merge when a narrower strategy would do. If you can describe the changed data with a predicate, replace_where does less work than a merge that has to scan the target to find matches. If you can't, incremental_predicates on the merge narrows that scan considerably. Every strategy above is a decision you make and have to maintain. The next practice lets the platform take care of this for you. Materialized views automate incrementalization. You can define the model as plain SQL, and Databricks tracks which underlying data has changed and refreshes only the affected results. On dbt-databricks, a materialized view is a native materialization , so this is a one-line config change: Materialized views fit best at the serving layer: aggregations over frequently changing sources, especially the expensive ones that back dashboards and need to stay fresh. In our TPC-DI benchmark, switching full recomputes to materialized views at the serving layer delivered 17x speedup. Choosing partition keys, reworking them when query patterns change, and scheduling OPTIMIZE , VACUUM , and ANALYZE in post-hooks all take engineering time. Predictive Optimization runs OPTIMIZE , VACUUM , and statistics collection on managed tables automatically, choosing what to run and when based on how each table is queried. Enable it once at the catalog or schema level, and the post-hooks that dbt projects usually accumulate for table maintenance can be retired. For data layout, Liquid Clustering replaces partition design with a self-tuning layout. It organizes data based on how the table is actually queried, sidesteps the small-file explosion that over-partitioned tables hit, and adapts as query patterns drift. Or let Databricks choose and adjust them from query history with automatic Liquid Clustering ( CLUSTER BY AUTO ), powered by Predictive Optimization. A single project-level config clusters every new table the project builds. Both features are designed as one-time decisions. With Automatic upgrades , Unity Catalog managed tables keep picking up new optimizations as Databricks ships them. At the end of the quarter, finance asks why the warehouse bill went up. In most setups nobody can answer, because a query in the usage data carries no connection to the dbt model that issued it. Query tags make the connection automatic. Every query dbt runs on Databricks is automatically stamped with the model name, dbt version, and materialization type. Add your own DIY custom tags for the dimensions your organization budgets by: The tags surface in system.query.history , and joining against system.billing.usage attributes serverless warehouse spend to any grouping the tags support: cost by model, by team, by domain, by materialization. You can see exactly which models cost the most. A typical dbt setup leans on a stack of other tools: a separate system to ingest the data, an external orchestrator to run the project, BI tools that each redefine the same metrics, and governance that lives outside your dbt project. Each is one more thing to maintain and one more place for things to drift. Adopt the practices in this section and one dbt project will: Ingestion is the part of the pipeline that has traditionally lived outside dbt, resulting in a split architecture with no single lineage overview. The streaming_table materialization removes that split. A dbt model materialized as a streaming table incrementally picks up new files or events as they arrive, so ingestion becomes just another model in the DAG. From there the rest of the pipeline (silver and gold models) can reference the streaming table with ref() , tests and documentation apply to every layer, and lineage covers the whole path from raw files to the final mart. Every BI tool, agent, or other consumer of data builds their own definitions of metrics, which leads to confusion and disagreement among stakeholders. A metric view moves the definition into one governed place: you declare the measures and dimensions once, and every consumer queries the same logic. dbt-databricks exposes metric views as a native materialization type, so the definition lives in your dbt project, versioned and reviewed like any other model. Users can pick their own groupings at query time with the MEASURE() function, so the same definition serves the SQL editor, BI dashboards, notebooks, and Genie. A dbt run is rarely the whole pipeline. When upstream and downstream steps live in different tools, the overhead adds up: additional tools to manage, pay for, and secure, with scattered lineage. Lakeflow Jobs collapses that into one Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with dbt as a native task . An ingestion task feeds the dbt task and downstream tasks trigger on completion, with dependencies enforced by the platform. The operational layer comes built in with scheduling, automatic retries, run history, and alerts, with no additional infrastructure to maintain. Jobs supports dbt Core and dbt Platform, and support for dbt Core v2.0 is on the way. A job assembled by hand in the UI is hard to version, review, or reproduce. Declarative Automation Bundles (DABs) fix this by making the job definition part of the code repository. Lakeflow Job, its schedule, compute settings, and the dbt project, all declared in YAML and deployed as one package. Deploying with --target dev creates an isolated copy of the whole pipeline; --target prod promotes it. Not every model within a project needs to run on every schedule. Tag models by cadence in dbt YAML and give each cadence its own job that builds only the models carrying its tag. Moving a model from daily to hourly becomes a one-line change: Governance is usually configured after your models run, separate from the dbt project that builds the data. Because governance sits outside your dbt project, it can drift out of sync with your dbt runs. Define governance in the dbt project where the models already live. As project config, it ships with the code, gets reviewed like the code, and Unity Catalog enforces it on every query. Tags, grants, and row and column-level protection all can be defined in project-wide config in dbt_project.yml .

title: llm-d 1.0 hardens open-source AI inference for production
abstract: Today at the PyTorch Conference North America, llm-d project contributors are announcing llm-d 1.0, a major milestone for open-source AI infrastructure. A Kubernetes-native distributed inference serving network , llm-d makes it possible to deploy inference stacks for any model, on any accelerator, in any cloud. The release signals that llm-d has moved beyond demonstrating individual performance techniques and is ready to support the realities of production: sustained efficiency under many workloads, all while balancing service priorities amid growing demand. And with inference costs increasing, llm-d is meant to help bring model deployment in-house and deliver returns on AI investment. The work has been developed with a growing open-source community that includes hardware providers, model developers, cloud platforms, and enterprise users. As lead maintainers of llm-d, Red Hat, IBM, and Google have helped turn advanced inference techniques into a coordinated system that enterprises can operate at scale. The three co-founded llm-d last year with CoreWeave and NVIDIA, and industry leaders including AMD, Cisco, Hugging Face, Intel, Lambda, and Mistral AI have joined as contributors along the way. The result is a vendor-neutral alternative for organizations that want frontier-class inference performance without depending entirely on one proprietary model provider, cloud, or hardware platform. “llm-d is ready for day 2 operations,” said Carlos Costa, Distinguished Engineer at IBM Research, llm-d co-founder and lead maintainer. “llm-d has been delivering state-of-the-art inference performance for production workloads. What 1.0 adds is the maturity to run it like any other critical service: a stable API, multiple tenants with competing priorities sharing the same infrastructure, and upgrades that don't interrupt operations. That is what we built llm-d 1.0 to do.” A full production stack Since llm-d launched, the project has focused on five important approaches to improving AI inference: prefix-cache-aware routing, which directs a request to infrastructure that may already hold its shared context; KV-cache offloading, which expands the useful life of cached information by moving it across GPU, CPU, and storage resources; batch inference optimization, which groups work so infrastructure can process it more efficiently; prefill/decode disaggregation, which separates the work of reading a prompt from the work of generating a response; and wide expert parallelism, which distributes large mixture-of-experts models across many accelerators. These ideas are not new to version 1.0. What is new is the level of integration and operational maturity around them. With version 1.0, llm-d has matured into a stack capable of supporting day 2 operations: everything that must happen after an AI service is deployed. That includes serving workloads with competing priorities, managing different performance requirements, maintaining efficiency, prioritizing important services, and keeping the system dependable over time. A benchmark can show that one feature improves throughput, but a production system must keep delivering that performance when traffic changes, hardware fails, software is updated, or different users compete for the same resources. llm-d 1.0 is about making the individual techniques work together under those less predictable conditions. One endpoint, different kinds of work Expanding on the core technical innovations that have already made llm-d a powerful tool for distributed inference, llm-d 1.0 enhances support for multi-tenant quality of service, zero-downtime operations, and agent-aware serving, for sustained performance in common day 2 production operations. An enterprise AI service may receive requests from people and autonomous agents through the same endpoint, but those workloads behave differently. A person using a coding assistant expects a fast answer. An agent may send a large burst of requests, pause while using a tool, and then return for another round of model calls. With flow control , llm-d 1.0 manages competing priorities whether workloads share the same hardware or span a mix of accelerators. Flow control, fairness, and prioritization help prevent bursty workloads from overwhelming latency-sensitive services. Under heavy demand, the system can make more deliberate decisions about which requests should receive resources first. Requests can also remain pinned to the appropriate infrastructure across multiple turns. That keeps their prefix caches warm, increasing the chance that previously processed context can be reused instead of calculated again. This matters for conversational assistants, but it is especially valuable for agents. Agents frequently return to the same code, documents, instructions, and conversation history while carrying out a task. Prefix-cache-aware routing sends each turn toward a replica that already holds the relevant context, while KV-cache offloading helps preserve more of that reusable information when GPU memory becomes constrained. This is what production readiness looks like in practice: serving a model more effectively and more cost-effectively by understanding the work arriving at that model and managing infrastructure accordingly. Improving AI ROI with better infrastructure This production focus leads directly to the economics of AI. As AI moves into everyday business operations, inference has become a recurring expense. Agentic systems can increase that expense because a single assignment may involve many rounds of reasoning, tool use, evaluation, and revision. If every step requires a model to reread the same material, you’re repeatedly paying for work the system has already done. In a recent test of an agentic coding workload, llm-d’s prefix-aware router captured 97% of the available cache reuse . By avoiding repeated computation and making more efficient use of existing hardware, techniques like this can reduce the cost of serving AI at scale. In another recent demonstration, IBM and Red Hat ran 3,000 software-engineering agents concurrently on a self-hosted deployment for 5 to 10 times less than the actual price of serving the same open model as a service. When an organization operates its own infrastructure, the infrastructure becomes part of a cost structure that can be managed. By combining open-weight models with an open serving stack, llm-d gives organizations another option for controlling the relationship between AI consumption, infrastructure spending, and business value. Connecting the open-source AI Ecosystem llm-d works with inference engines such as vLLM or SGLang , adding the distributed routing and operational capabilities needed to turn model servers into production services. That also gives llm-d an important role in the broader open-source ecosystem. PyTorch is closely associated with the people developing AI models and applications. The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), which hosts llm-d as a sandbox project, focuses more heavily on deploying and operating systems in production. The llm-d project is a bridge between these worlds. “llm-d unifies the PyTorch and CNCF ecosystems by bringing Kubernetes-native orchestration directly to vLLM and modern inference engines,” said Stephen Watt, vice president, office of the chief technology officer, Red Hat. “It delivers high-performance, distributed inference with the reliability and scale enterprises need — all within an operational model they already know.” IBM’s contribution to llm-d reflects a long-standing approach: Take ideas that can improve computing and turn them into open technologies that organizations can use in the real world. With llm-d 1.0, that work has helped produce an inference stack designed not only to perform well, but to keep performing when AI becomes critical infrastructure. Open-source AI inference is ready to be operated, governed, and optimized in production.

title: Meta drops the word "train" from its commercial TOS after AI backlash
abstract: Hoping to quell criticism, Meta has dropped the word “train” from its “streamlined” commercial terms of service that kick in on October 30. Last week, Meta faced backlash after legal experts warned that the tech giant’s sweeping new commercial terms of service seemed to give Meta permission to endlessly scrape websites linked on business pages. Talking to Nieman Lab, experts suggested that Meta could possibly use the policy to avoid millions in licensing fees from news organizations by requiring all business users to share a wealth of AI training data simply for running a business page. A Meta spokesperson confirmed that Meta did not alert users to the changed language following backlash. This potentially only adds to confusion ahead of the policy roll-out. In response to backlash, Meta's spokesperson provided a statement to Ars, acknowledging Nieman Lab's initial report but not its follow-up report reiterating experts' concerns:

title: Gemini's Personal Intelligence is coming to cars
abstract: Google kicked off 2026 with the addition of Personal Intelligence to Gemini, allowing its AI to pull in more of your data to formulate answers. It started as a paid feature but eventually came to all Gemini users. However, this feature wasn't available in the car until now. Google is rolling out Personal Intelligence to Android Auto and Google Built-in, and it is still, thankfully, an optional feature. As Google points out , a generative AI's outputs are better "when it knows the world and knows you," which is correct in an uncomfortable sort of way. The more context you can provide to a model, the better the output will be at the end of the token shuffle. Since Google has so much of your data already, it sees Personal Intelligence as a differentiator versus other AI systems. You don't have to provide the AI context because it already has it from apps like Gmail and Calendar. Personal Intelligence is beginning its rollout in Android Auto today, and it will come to vehicles with Google built-in in the next few months. As an aside, "Google built-in" is questionable branding, but it refers to cars that run Google software in the infotainment system rather than projecting an interface from your phone. Very few vehicles have Google built-in, but Google often releases new car features on them first. This time, it's the other way around.

title: Ukraine’s drone rescue of wounded soldier puts much touted idea into practice
abstract: Ukraine’s unprecedented drone rescue of a wounded soldier from the battlefield has shown once again how battlefield necessity can spur innovation. The operation was revealed just days after separate Ukrainian drones designed for casualty evacuation were deployed for frontline testing—taking a step beyond the US military’s decades of experimentation with similar concepts. The drone evacuation of the injured soldier took place at an undisclosed time and place on the frontline where the presence of Russian drones and landmines made it impractical to send in a wheeled ground robot , according to The Kyiv Independent . On October 19, Ukraine’s Army shared a video of the drone evacuation, showing the wounded soldier securing himself in a harness suspended beneath a heavy hexacopter drone with six rotors before being flown to safety. “This is a historic event, the next stage of evacuating the wounded, which we will all come to,” said Napalm, a programmer of the 92nd separate assault brigade's unmanned ground systems company, who went by his callsign per Ukrainian military practice, in a statement. “Now the serious systematic work begins, so that such missions are carried out constantly.”

title: Meta tries to scapegoat staff who downloaded torrents to spare execs
abstract: In copyright lawsuits over AI training, Meta has spent weeks blaming staff for downloading torrents. The company has now been ordered to name executives who authorized decisions to pirate books from shadow libraries like Anna’s Archive and LibGen, TorrentFreak reported . In a discovery order impacting a class action raised by book authors—including Richard Kadrey and Sarah Silverman—as well as a lawsuit from publisher Entrepreneur Media, Magistrate Judge Thomas Hixon largely agreed that Meta must clearly identify key decision-makers. Following testimony from Meta staff who downloaded torrents, the order could expose a wider range of supervisors, managers, and executives whom staffers said greenlit the piracy. Meta had been hoping to avoid detailing the chain of command, particularly for leadership involved in early AI training. According to a Meta court filing , its initial efforts to compile massive AI datasets were managed through an “informal approach" where supposedly nobody with authority made any decisions. Instead, Meta insisted that a “decision” was “made only in the sense” that some staffers “technically” downloaded torrents.

title: Meta Muse exposes users' personal and business secrets when they share conversations
abstract: Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it's suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including:

title: NotebookLM's Video Overview System Prompt: The Full Creation Workflow
abstract:
The Video Overview creation skill shared below lays out a complete workflow for turning notebook sources into a video: read the context, help the user choose a focus, confirm the settings, and hand the request to the video generation pipeline. What caught my attention is how much of the prompt deals with getting the user's intent right. It distinguishes a new video request from a question about an existing one, discards abandoned choices when the user starts over, and preserves the user's approved focus text verbatim when submitting the generation request. The file also includes the questionnaire and review card schemas, format and visual style rules, localization requirements, and example tool calls. Those schemas and calls reference NotebookLM-specific components and tools; they describe the orchestration layer rather than a standalone prompt to paste into a video customization box. Below is the full supplied skill file, reproduced unchanged in one code block, including its metadata, JSON templates, and dispatch examples. ---
name: vo-creation
description: >- Create cinematic videos from content using a multi-step co-creation workflow. Use when user wants a breakdown, cinematic video, or movie-style video overview from their sources.
--- # Video Creation You are a World-Class Video Producer and Visual Storyteller. Your goal is to
transform raw sources into a cinematic breakdown video using a co-creation and
multi-step agentic workflow. Your tone should be like a thoughtful creative
partner. ## Context Gathering (IMPORTANT) Prefill every card field from context you already have. Make a tool call only
when that context falls short: 1. **Source material**: Use the source summaries already in the notebook context to identify themes and topics. Only run a `semantic_search` (at most once) if the summaries are insufficient — for example, when a selected source has no summary, when the summaries are too brief to extract 3 distinct themes, or when the user asks about a specific section or detail not covered in the summaries (e.g., "chapter 3"). Do not call `semantic_search` if the summaries already provide enough detail to populate the card.
2. **Conversation history**: Review the full conversation. Pay **special attention to the user's last message** — it often contains the most specific and recent intent signal (e.g., "make a breakdown about the economic impact section" or "cinematic video on chapter 3").
3. **Implicit preferences**: Infer tone, audience, and visual feel from context clues. A scientific paper suggests a grounded, analytical tone; a pop-culture topic suggests something vibrant and energetic. Use this context to prefill every field in the cards below. The user should be
able to hit "Generate" on the Review Card immediately and get a great result. ## User Intent Resolution & Disambiguation (CRITICAL) Before deciding which card to show or what action to take, you **must resolve
the user's intent** by examining their latest message in relation to any
existing artifacts or in-progress cards: ### 1. Existing Artifact vs. New Co-Creation Journey - **Referring to an existing artifact**: If an artifact has already been generated or is currently generating in the notebook/session (e.g., in the Studio panel), and the user is asking about it (e.g., "how is my video?", "check on the video", "show me the video", "can you change the style of that video?"): - Respond conversationally about the existing artifact and direct them to the Studio panel. - **Do NOT** show a new card or call `create_artifact`.
- **Starting a new co-creation journey**: If the user explicitly wants a new artifact or a new topic (e.g., "make me a video", "make another video", "create a video about X", "generate a new video"): - Treat this as a brand-new, independent request. - Do NOT carry forward unrelated settings or topics from previous artifacts. - If a video already exists, mention it in one line ("Your video 'X' is in Studio. Let's set up a new one.") and continue to Step 0 or Step 1.
- **No creation verb** (e.g., just "video?" or "the video") while a video exists: answer about that video and offer a new one in the same reply.
- **Let the card carry open choices.** If the notebook covers several topics or angles, show the Questionnaire Card with them as focus chips instead of asking in chat. Ask in chat only when no card can express the choice (e.g., the notebook has no sources). ### 2. Handling "Start Over" & Card Abandonment - If a Questionnaire Card or Review Card is currently pending/unsubmitted in chat, and the user sends a message indicating they want to start over, try again, or create a different video (e.g., "generate a new video", "start over", "start again", "make another video", "new video", "let's try again", "scratch that"): - **Treat the previous card as ABANDONED.** - **PURGE all previous selections**: Discard all prior format choices, focus chips, topic titles, and style selections from the abandoned card. **Never carry forward abandoned preferences.** - **Evaluate the new request as fresh**: - If the user provided a specific new topic (e.g., "start over and make a video on photosynthesis"), gather context for that new topic and present Step 0 or Step 1 for it. - If the user did NOT provide a topic (e.g., just "generate a new video", "start over"), the request is underspecified — **you MUST present Step 0: Questionnaire Card**. Never skip Step 0 by recycling the abandoned topic! - **Never call `create_artifact`**: An abandoned card must never trigger generation. ## Translation & Localization (CRITICAL) All human-facing display strings across both QuestionnaireCard and
CoCreationReviewCard A2UI components MUST be translated into the user's active
device/conversation language (e.g., Spanish, French, German, Japanese, etc.). ### What MUST be translated into the user's active language: - **Card Titles**: e.g., `"Let's set up your video"`, `"Video: <Topic>"`
- **Question Text & Subtitles**: e.g., `"What should the format be?"`, `"What should the video focus on?"`, `"Select 1 or 2 topics for a sharper video"`
- **Option Labels & Descriptions**: e.g., `"Explainer"`, `"Comprehensive overview that connects the dots"`, `"Short"`, `"Bite-sized overview to help quickly grasp core ideas"`, `"Cinematic"`, `"Engaging, expressive content that dives deep"`
- **Focus Chip Labels**: Dynamic and pre-selected focus topics
- **Review Notice Text**: Title, label, and expanded label (e.g., `"Review producer notes"`, `"Review producer notes before final rendering"`, `"Refine draft producer notes before final generation..."`)
- **Any other human-readable display strings** presented to the user in the UI. ### What MUST NOT be translated (Preserve structural identifiers): - Schema keys and property names (e.g., `surfaceId`, `catalogId`, `component`, `id`, `icon`, `imageEnum`, `selectionType`, `subtitle`, `subtitleVisibleOptions`, `options`, `questions`, `styleList`, `selectedStyle`, `styleVisibleFormats`, `reviewNotice`)
- Structural IDs and enum values (e.g., `"root"`, `"QuestionnaireCard"`, `"CoCreationReviewCard"`, `"explainer"`, `"short"`, `"cinematic"`, `"crop_16_9"`, `"crop_9_16"`, `"movie"`, `"stylus_note_spark"`, `"subscriptions"`, `"vo_styles"`, `"auto_select"`, `"en"`, `"es"`, `"fr"`, `"de"`, `"ja"`, `"ko"`, `"pt"`, `"zh"`, etc.) > **OVERRIDE NOTICE:** This Translation & Localization clause overrides any
> directive to copy text in quotes as-is. While structural identifiers, keys,
> IDs, icons, and enums must be preserved as-is, all human-readable display
> strings must be translated into the active device/conversation language. ## Step 0: Co-Creation Questionnaire Card (Conditional) Decide using the **whole active journey**, not just the latest message. If the
user is answering a question you asked, read the answer together with their
original request.

title: Battle Drones—a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
abstract: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones ( play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I’m somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to “Make it a LOT more fun”. It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here’s what I’ve built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer . I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. Here’s a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser: Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded—I’ve reviewed almost none of the code, and it’s built in a language (TypeScript) that I’ve hardly used myself. I’ve playtested it quite a bit though, and it’s been through a large number of iterations since I started the project. Here’s a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts. I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July: We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions Here’s a shared transcript . I’d given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites. You can try v1 here —it looked like this: It’s recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against. This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn’t any fun to play. Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn’t even realize this until several iterations later! The second version ( try v2 here ) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the “AI vs. AI” mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself. Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI’s image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder. It still wasn’t much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it: Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain. This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here . Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here —it looks like this: This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn’t very fun to play though—I found myself getting bored pretty quickly. So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can’t actually make something that’s genuinely compelling to play. I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone: This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun. This time I was running in Ultracode mode , where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs “dynamic workflows”, described in their docs as: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once. This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn’t get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular. You can try v4 here —it looks like this: I had Claude write its own release notes —here are the highlights: Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that’s losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play. Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%. Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features. After the success of Ultracode at “Make it a LOT more fun”, I decided to be more ambitious: Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version : The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code. v6 ( play v6 here ) added some more visual polish. v7 ( play v7 ) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a “Condor” troop carrying aircraft. I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game—it really had been a case of me saying “make it more fun” and “add visual polish” for the past few releases. I’d noticed that the AI didn’t use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often—there wasn’t a great strategic reason to use them. It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map. This resulted in my longest prompt yet: Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles. To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor. Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board. The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different places I want to encourage a battle over uplinks. The map should be the times the size of other maps - still square First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications You get to design a new biome for this The result was the tropical Archipelago map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It’s definitely the most fun map to play, once you’ve got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting—it now looks like this: I decided to add giant robot mechs to the game—think Jaegers from Pacific Rim , or Titans from Warhammer 40,000. Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude: Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnoughts or titans from W20K - how could we do this in a way that enhanced gameplay, kept things balanced, added unique twist? Don't overthink this yet Let's keep brainstorming. I like the idea that it's a mobile base - that can accept harvested scrap and can have buildings built near it (even if it later moves on) and can produce infantry units too.

title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
abstract: Python 3.15 is here ! Here’s the essential What’s new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. I’m most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here’s an illustration lifted from the documentation : PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448 , which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015. Python’s existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing , and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling . Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They’re very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first. I’ve previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library. If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS): Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this: It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this , and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI. Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase. Miguel’s explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories. I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release: Then I installed the stable 3.15 release: And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version: Now the following reports 3.15 as the version: I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install . I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this: Then I can confirm the version like this: The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported . My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11. Here’s the What’s new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available! Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio . 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout() , and several more new features. datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc . Python’s SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including: Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python’s typing system . I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here’s my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround. I’ve also updated my click-app , datasette-plugin , python-lib , and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15. This is Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11 by Simon Willison, posted on 12th October 2026 .
