title: The US orders every civilian agency to rip out DeepSeek, even tools built on it
abstract:
Markwayne Mullin in his official US Senate portrait, taken before he became Homeland Security Secretary. Image: United States Senate / Wikimedia Commons, Public domain, cropped The US government has ordered every federal civilian agency to strip DeepSeek out of its computers and stop buying it, along with any third-party product built on the Chinese lab's AI. The Department of Homeland Security filed notice of the order with the Federal Register on Monday, under a 2018 supply chain law that lets it bar risky technology from government systems. The order, numbered 2026-01 and signed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, is dated July 24, 2026. It was kept out of public view until this week. Its notice is due to appear in the Federal Register on Tuesday, October 20, under docket DHS-2026-0628. What the DeepSeek ban covers The order tells all civilian agencies to do two things. First, exclude Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence, its affiliates and their products from purchasing "effective immediately", including agency-approved product lists, e-commerce marketplaces and similar buying channels. Second, remove products from DeepSeek and its affiliates, "and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations", from agency IT systems immediately. That second clause is the wide one. DeepSeek's models are released as open weights, so they turn up inside other companies' tools as well as in DeepSeek's own app and website. The order does not list which products it means, and it does not say how agencies should treat a DeepSeek model running on a US company's servers. It also comes days after DeepSeek updated its cheap Flash model , which it says now beats Claude Opus 5 at some coding tasks. It does not reach the military or spy agencies. The order applies to federal civilian executive branch agencies "except for their national security systems and secure compartmented information systems", which fall under the Pentagon and the Director of National Intelligence. "Multiple threat vectors": why DHS says DeepSeek is a risk The order's summary of risks says DeepSeek's servers are in China and that Chinese law "permits extensive authority to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private company infrastructure". It says DeepSeek's sign-up process collects personal information and may "track and digitally fingerprint users", and that its apps work by having people type in information, which could mean sensitive data from US government staff or contractors ends up in China. Combined with public data, that information "could produce actionable intelligence on U.S. persons and/or government programs", the order says. It adds that the models "may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities", and cites a February 2025 NowSecure audit that found multiple critical flaws in DeepSeek's iPhone app. The order's evidence is drawn from public material: DeepSeek's own privacy policy, a 2020 DHS business advisory on Chinese data risks and an April 2025 House Select Committee on China report. It doesn't describe any case of government data reaching DeepSeek. Exceptions and the 60-day window Agencies that can't comply can ask for an exception, such as having the order not apply to them, to certain actions, or a delay. Requests must be made in writing within 60 days of the order's issue, with a "compelling justification", for example the impact on mission-critical work, and any alternative safeguards. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) reviews them and approves or refuses in writing. Until DeepSeek products are gone, agencies are told to monitor traffic in and out of their networks, step up logging, add controls against data leaving their systems and flag anything unusual. CISA can help agencies that lack the skills to comply, and the Secretary must review the order within a year and every year after. DeepSeek bans around the world Several parts of the US government already blocked DeepSeek on their own devices, including the Commerce Department and the Navy, as did states including New York, Tennessee and Virginia, Reuters reported. Abroad, Italy's data protection authority blocked the DeepSeek app in early 2025, and Taiwan, South Korea and Australia barred it from government devices. Monday's order goes further, covering every civilian agency and everything they buy. DeepSeek hasn't commented. The Chinese embassy in Washington didn't immediately comment, according to Reuters. The order lands as Beijing tightens its own grip on the sector: China now wants to control exports of its largest AI models, and DeepSeek is training its next model on Chinese chips . Why it matters This is the US government's broadest move yet against a Chinese AI lab, and by reaching third-party tools built on DeepSeek it puts the burden on every vendor selling AI to federal agencies to know which models sit inside their products. Chinese open models are among the most downloaded in the world, and few publish safety results at launch , so expect more buyers to start asking the same question. Sources: Department of Homeland Security, "Notice of Order Regarding Exclusion and Removal of DeepSeek Products from Federal Civilian Executive Branch Information Technology Systems and Procurements" and Exclusion and Removal Order #2026-01 (Federal Register public inspection, document 2026-21447) ; Reuters (earlier bans and embassy response). title: NixOS is making me less afraid
abstract:
On the go? Listen to an ai -narrated version of this article . Confused? More about ai narration . Something funny happened a little while ago: I read about FreshRSS, and it
sounded nice, so I installed it on a server and started using it . That would
not have happened a year ago, but then again, a year ago I didn’t have any NixOS
servers. For the past few years, my rss feeds have lived locally on my phone only.
There was a good idea behind that 1 1 I can mostly take time to read when I’m
away from my computer anyway. , but it never quite worked in practice. For one,
many things are easier to read on a larger screen. But it was also brittle to
trust a phone app to manage the read/unread status of thousands of articles
across a hundred feeds. 2 2 In particular, when I switched to a different phone
I could migrate all feeds to it, but the read/unread status was lost along the
way. What I really wanted was a server-side feed aggregator. This is software
that runs on a server, manages rss feeds, and then I can read the rss feeds
either through a web interface, or through client applications. I’ve wanted that
for a while, but I’ve never taken the step, because it would be yet another side
project to maintain the deployment of. But now, with some NixOS experience, adding a working FreshRSS configuration
(including backups) took 9 lines of Nix code 3 3 Plus a dozen more lines for the
nginx reverse proxy configuration. It got a little complicated because I wanted
to proxy_pass from a specific location block which required rewriting cookie
paths. But that’s a me problem, not a NixOS problem. . That installation has
just hands-off worked for the past few months. If or when that server breaks, I
can spin up a new one running the exact same configuration, probably in
something like 15 minutes. When we can do something like that, there is
literally no reason to not just try the new software. Contrast this against how FreshRSS is installed outside of NixOS. Then we’d download and extract an archive to the right location; configure permissions according to instructions; install nginx and php-fpm with necessary extra dependencies to the server; configure php-fpm pools and make nginx pass requests through to php-fpm ; set up Let’s Encrypt certificates; set up backups; and hopefully remember how to do all the above if something breaks and we need to
reinstall FreshRSS on a new or upgraded server later. Of course, the FreshRSS project provides a container image which would shorten
the process a little bit. It purports to set up Apache with mod_php and
configure them the right way. Then we’d only need to configure backups, create a
systemd service that runs the container, and manage nginx as a tls terminating
reverse proxy in front of that, because the container image reasonably does not
come with tls support. This is still stuff to remember, and there’s also no
guarantee the same thing works six months down the line when reinstalling,
unless we wrote down which exact container image we downloaded. 4 4 It does not
help to build the container image from source, because two builds from the same
Dockerfile separated by time can result in rather different container images. I have mentioned before how much I dislike maintaining side projects. That
includes my own code, but also self-hosted services developed by someone else.
I’m okay with a few minutes of maintenance here and there, but having to
schedule hours of uninterrupted work to upgrade something, or spending any amount of time at all on emergency maintenance, really kills my desire to work
with computers. You’d think someone of my disposition would be deep into configuration
management, container orchestration, or both, but no. I have made honest
attempts with CFEngine, Ansible, podman, and k3s but none of them improved my
installation/configuration/deployment experience significantly over (a)
carefully writing things down, and sometimes (b) turning those careful notes
into a shell script performing a sequence of ssh commands. 5 5 Yes, this is
essentially reinventing Ansible – but less brittle. It won’t break the next time
someone glances sideways at pip . The drawback of the shell script is that it
often ends up relying on assumptions that become invalid with time, or when it
is used in a different environment. A NixOS configuration reads a lot like the
careful instructions to myself, except they’re executable and they produce the
same result every time.

title: Methodology for the application of generative artificial intelligence tools in higher design education
abstract: The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) technologies across both theoretical and practical domains is fundamentally transforming the epistemological and pedagogical foundations of higher design education. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the methodological integration of generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, Claude, Midjourney, and DALL·E, in fostering creative thinking, critical analysis, and practical skills among design students in higher education institutions. The research examines the transition of studio pedagogy from traditional forms toward hybrid and dialogical models, the reinterpretation of Donald Schön’s concept of reflection-in-action within algorithmic environments, and the evolving role of the educator in AI-assisted learning processes. Methodologically, the study is grounded in a modified Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework and a four-component Information and Communication Competence (ICC) model. The findings indicate that the systematic and purposeful implementation of GAI tools can increase students’ visual design production and productivity by approximately 14%; however, it may also lead to reduced diversity of ideas and an overreliance on algorithms for cognitive functions. To mitigate these risks, the study proposes the concepts of epistemic vigilance and process-oriented hybrid assessment mechanisms as essential components of contemporary design education.

title: Data drift monitoring in the maintenance of cascade software for detecting falsified digital information
abstract: The article considers the maintenance stage of cascade software for detecting falsified digital information, in which inexpensive classifiers resolve most messages and pass uncertain ones to a large language model. After deployment, the distribution of messages changes because of new narratives, new text generators and deliberate adaptation of adversaries, while true labels arrive with a delay or not at all. A system of seven monitoring signals is proposed, each linked to a component of the cascade and to the type of drift it reveals, and only one of them requires true labels. It is shown that in a cascade a covariate shift manifests primarily as growth of the escalation share, so that quality may remain stable while processing cost increases. To detect confident errors of the first tier that leave the escalation share unchanged, shadow escalation of a small random sample of first-tier decisions is proposed. An alarm rule based on non-overlapping confidence intervals and a graded response policy, from threshold recalibration to retraining and rollback, are described.

title: Trustworthy Phishing URL Detection Using Machine Learning: Performance Analysis and Future Directions
abstract: Over the years, Uniform Resource Locator (URL) Phishing has been a threat to online security because their scams exploit trust in a misleading URL to trick unsuspecting users into disclosing their username or passwords and other personal information. Not only that, but it is also crucial to identify these malicious URLs and ensure online platforms and users are protected. The ISCXURL2016 data was utilized for the purpose of analyzing the performance of different Machine Learning (ML) models in differentiating phishing and legitimate URLs in this paper. A wide range of classifiers were explored including the classic classifiers as well as more advanced ensemble classifiers. The results of the experiments indicate that ensemble-based boosting models can be more beneficial for URL phishing detection. HistGradientBoost achieved the highest accuracy of 98.47%, followed closely by LightGBM and XGBoost that both outperformed the accuracy of 98%. The other classifiers, RandomForest and ExtraTrees, also performed well with accuracy above 97% and traditional classifiers such as Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) showed the poorest performance with an accuracy of 67.75%. The results show that the boosting-based ensembles provide a suitable negation of the complex and non-linear structure of phishing URLs. Along with empirical evaluation, it offers a Properties & Positioning viewpoint as well as the importance of the ML-based phishing detection in the broader context of cybersecurity issues. Moreover, it discusses the future directions, with Federated Learning (FL) in the context of decentralized and privacy-preserving collaboration and Large Language Models (LLM) in the context of semantic reasoning and flexibility. These insights together will provide the building blocks for more intelligent, adaptive and trustworthy phishing organizations.

title: Cross-media affective differences in online reviews: aspect-level evidence and a dual-pathway mechanism
abstract:
This study investigates the micro-level structural differences in online review affect between social media and e-commerce platforms, exploring the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive consumers to selectively express polarised reviews across these media.
 
 
 
 Utilising large language model-driven aspect-based sentiment analysis, this study quantifies an initial dataset of 65,493 smartphone online reviews from TikTok, Bilibili, Jingdong and Suning to identify aspect-level affective differences. To explain the observed differences, Study 2 draws on uses and gratifications theory and conducts a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment, using wireless headphones as the focal product and TikTok and Taobao as the platforms, to examine how media environments moderate the translation of consumption experiences into review intentions.
 
 
 
 Affective differences extend to specific cognitive attributes, with social media platforms exhibiting a significantly more negative and heterogeneous affective landscape, whereas e-commerce platforms demonstrate overwhelming positivity. These differences are driven by a dual-pathway mechanism. Social media platforms primarily activate self-enhancement motivation, which facilitates the translation of negative experiences into negative reviews while weakening the translation of positive experiences into positive reviews. Conversely, e-commerce platforms primarily activate economic motivation, which facilitates the translation of positive experiences into positive reviews while reducing the likelihood of negative experiences translating into negative reviews.
 
 
 
 This study extends the investigation of review affect from within-medium comparisons to cross-media analysis. By shifting from macro-level indicators to micro-level attribute evidence, this study reveals a more comprehensive picture of cross-media affective bias. By extending the application of uses and gratifications theory from content consumption to content production, it offers a novel mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon.

title: CODA: Cohort- and Drift-aware Foundation Model for Multimodal Clinical Reasoning
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have demonstrated strong performance across diverse clinical tasks. However, existing approaches predominantly operate at the individual sample level and fail to model the interplay between population-level cohort patterns and patient-specific variation that underlie real-world clinical reasoning. In practice, clinicians routinely reason through patient cohorts sharing similar demographic, physiological, or pathological characteristics, while accounting for patient-specific deviations from the group prototype. Motivated by this gap, we propose CODA, a cohort- and drift-aware foundation model for multimodal clinical reasoning. CODA explicitly integrates cohort structure into the modeling pipeline through two complementary mechanisms: cohort-aware population stratification and drift-aware individual adaptation. In particular, we leverage reinforcement learning to discover clinically meaningful patient cohorts, and further model each patient's deviation from cohort prototypes as a structured drift signal encoding fine-grained individual heterogeneity. These cohort- and drift-aware representations are incorporated into the foundation model to enable reasoning that is simultaneously informed by population-level patterns and sensitive to individual-level variation. Extensive experiments on real-world electronic health record (EHR) benchmarks demonstrate that CODA achieves consistent effectiveness and strong generalizability across diverse clinical tasks, including closed-QA, open-QA, and report generation.

title: How Benchmark Graph Construction Shapes Multi-Hop KG Navigation: A Controlled Audit of PathQuestion and PathQuestion-Large
abstract: Multi-hop knowledge-graph question answering (KGQA) benchmarks are often treated as fixed language-and-reasoning tasks, but for navigation-based methods, difficulty also depends on the graph in which those tasks are instantiated. This makes graph construction a consequential but often entangled part of the navigation task. To isolate this effect, we audit PathQuestion (PQ) and PathQuestion-Large (PQL) as graph-navigation benchmarks under a controlled intervention: we hold questions, topic entities, released answers, released path annotations, and family-level splits fixed while replacing each released task-filtered graph with the larger source KG distributed with the benchmark. Source restoration expands the effective navigation search space and graph-consistent answer and path multiplicity while sharply reducing unguided reachability to released answers. We evaluate whether these structural changes persist across navigation policies using structural references, frozen small-language-model navigation policies, and trained MINERVA policies. Across both frozen and trained policies, restoration substantially reduces released-answer accuracy and trajectory fidelity, while graph-consistent evaluation recovers only part of the loss. These results show that benchmark graph construction is part of the navigation task specification rather than merely an implementation detail and can materially shape measured behavior even when the released QA task is held fixed.

title: Truncated Reasoning Under a Budget: Evaluating System-1 Models as Decision-makers
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate more reasoning tokens than needed. Limiting the reasoning budget reduces cost, but forcing an answer from an incomplete trace can hurt accuracy. System-1 decision models select among candidate options without producing a reasoning response. We evaluate Jev as a decision reader of truncated reasoning across seven LLM reasoners and five multiple-choice benchmarks (35 pairs). Jev achieves higher mean accuracy than forced answering at tested budgets from 500 to 16,000 tokens, including the estimated costs of reasoning and answering. At a 1,500-token budget, it improves accuracy by 4.1 pp overall and 8.6 pp on truncated questions, with significant gains in 17 pairs under Holm-corrected bootstrap tests. Offline replay estimates 34.5% of the full-run cost, with a 1.13 pp accuracy loss. A policy selected on training folds saves 71.3% of the estimated full-run cost on held-out folds, with a 0.58 pp accuracy loss. We also find that Jev shows strong question-only accuracy, exceeding 500-token forced answering on average (68.0% vs. 65.5%), although this advantage varies by benchmark. These findings suggest that System-1 decision models can complement LLM reasoning and reduce the need for costly reasoning completion.

title: Maestro: Agentic Formal Proof Development by Coordination
abstract: Lean is increasingly used to verify mathematical proofs and software produced by LLM agents, but writing formal proofs remains hard. Existing prover systems take a divide-and-conquer approach that recursively decomposes hard proof obligations into easier lemmas and splits again any lemma that resists proof. However, a lemma can resist proof for different reasons, including insufficient guidance, a false statement, or a flaw in the decomposition that produced it. Existing systems cannot tell these apart as a failed attempt reports little beyond its failure, and responses are confined to the failing node without considering the rest of the proof or revising the plan above it. The system may thus keep decomposing obligations along a flawed proof direction until the budget runs out, causing the whole proof attempt to fail. We introduce Maestro, a Lean prover harness that handles failures through global coordination. Provers report why they failed, not just that they failed, and a coordinator that sees the whole proof chooses an appropriate response, such as guiding a stuck prover, correcting a false lemma, or retracting a flawed subtree and replanning it. The same harness extends to verified code synthesis, where a checked counterexample sends the code back for repair. We evaluate Maestro with four frontier LLMs on seven mathematics and three software verification benchmarks. It proves more targets than each model's native coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) on every benchmark the agent has not already saturated, with the largest gains on research-level mathematics. With Claude Opus 5, it discovers its own proofs of 34 of the 48 theorems in the June 2026 release of arXivLean, against 19 for the native agent. It also outperforms all published prover systems on every benchmark they share, solving 669/672 PutnamBench, 59/60 Lean-IMO-Bench, and 6/6 IMO 2026.

title: From Tasks to Turns: Measuring Human Labor Contributions in Human-Agent Joint Production
abstract: In agent workflows, a brief human instruction can alter subsequent search, reasoning, and tool execution, yet final task outcomes rarely reveal the contribution of an individual instruction to human-agent joint production. We propose a Human Turn-level framework for measuring human contributions, using task quality and token usage to characterize the collaborative production outcomes associated with each human instruction. We compare continuations from adjacent checkpoints under matched models, budgets, and termination conditions, and assess stability through repeated measurements. Across four archived and simulated interaction settings, we conduct 29,124 comparisons between predicted and observed directions of quality and computational change at both Human Turn and session levels. On HumanBench, we obtain 506 valid comparisons across 85 real-user scenarios. Results show that quality and computational changes associated with human guidance depend on task conditions. Expert-style and ordinary-style guidance differ in information provision, correction, and repetition. Even when task quality after continuation is identical, remaining computational demands can differ substantially across checkpoints. Our framework advances the measurement of human labor contributions from tasks and sessions to individual turns, providing a repeatable, fine-grained foundation for studying human contributions and their allocation in human-agent joint production.
